Article Title: In 1999, Steven Spielberg and Kate Capshaw bought a 2.8-acre Los Angeles horse ranch for $5.75 million; 27 years later, their seven-bedroom equestrian estate with a 20,000-sq-ft riding arena is seekin
Article Text: In 1999, filmmaker Steven Spielberg and his wife, Kate Capshaw, purchased a sprawling ranch in Los Angeles through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million. Now, according to a report by Realtor.com, the couple has listed the property for nearly $30 million, decades after abandoning controversial plans to transform it with an enormous five-story riding facility.At the time, the Hollywood mogul, 79 and actress, 72, unveiled ambitious plans to dramatically overhaul the estate with a 27,000-square-foot, five-story riding facility featuring a domed roof and underground horse stables. The 'Jaws' director also reportedly envisioned more than $7 million worth of renovations, along with plans to construct a 2,400-square-foot guesthouse and a three-story guardhouse.However, the proposed transformation sparked a fierce backlash from their neighbours, who objected to the scale of the project. Although the Oscar-winning director reportedly planned to present revised ideas to his neighbours, the elaborate project ultimately never came to fruition. However, he did get a chance to update the estate into the magnificent abode it is today.The property has remained a part of Spielberg and Capshaw's extensive real estate portfolio for nearly three decades. Now, the couple is finally ready to part ways with the equestrian retreat, listing it for $29.9 million with Sandro Dazzan of The Agency.Known as Dogwood, the seven-bedroom, 9.5-bathroom estate sits on 2.8 acres in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon and offers an impressive array of equestrian amenities alongside its luxurious living spaces. Spanning two parcels, the property combines a sophisticated country-inspired aesthetic with extensive facilities designed for horses, entertaining and guests. Inside the main residence, rich walnut floors and wood-covered ceilings create a warm atmosphere, while expansive windows bring in plenty of natural light.The spacious living room offers multiple seating areas anchored by dual fireplaces, creating an inviting space for relaxing and entertaining. The chef's kitchen features extensive wood cabinetry, an oversized centre island, high-end appliances and an eat-in dining nook. "The chef's kitchen with eat-in dining nook and wood-burning fireplace connects to a cosy family room and IPE-clad terrace overlooking a tranquil reflection pond," the listing notes.Upstairs, the primary suite offers a peaceful retreat complete with a wood-burning fireplace and access to a private covered terrace. The outdoor space boasts yet another fireplace along with sweeping city and canyon views, according to the listing. Elsewhere inside the home is a media room that can double as a game room, as well as a wine cellar.Apart from all this, the property's most impressive feature is its four-legged residents. Across from the main entertaining spaces sits a six-stall barn complete with an executive office, staff quarters, three grooming stations, a feed kitchen and storage. The equestrian facility is topped off by a sprawling 20,000-square-foot riding arena with an observation deck and mirrored wall, which the listing notes is suitable for both dressage and jumping.The estate's lower parcel expands the compound even further with a stylish one-bedroom guesthouse equipped with its own kitchen, rooftop deck, and basement office and storage spaces. There is also a second four-stall barn, a 5,400-square-foot turnout area, a private gate, and enough parking for more than 10 vehicles. Both parcels are supported by a security command post and generators, further adding to the property's private compound-like feel.Outside, the ranch is surrounded by lush landscaping, while a tranquil reflection pond adds to its secluded, countryside atmosphere, despite the estate's location in the heart of Los Angeles."Nestled in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon, Dogwood is Los Angeles' premier equestrian ranch - a rare masterpiece designed by renowned architect Michael Kovac with interiors by Michael Smith and landscape design by Christine London," the listing states.
Article Summary: In 1999, Steven Spielberg and his wife, Kate Capshaw, purchased a sprawling ranch in Los Angeles for $5.75 million. At the time, the Hollywood mogul unveiled ambitious plans to dramatically overhaul the estate with a 27,000-square-foot, five-story riding facility. The proposed transformation sparked a fierce backlash from their neighbours, who objected to the scale of the project.

Article Title: A methane leak in the South China Sea formed a plume over 1km high; but bacteria and worms built a 'worm bed' within two years shocking scientists and theories
Article Text:
Oceanic burps

Clean-up time

After effects

There is a vast amount of methane trapped beneath the seafloor, across the planet. If it were to be released, the results could be potentially catastrophic for all forms of life. This is why finding out how ecosystems respond to methane leaks is important to ocean scientists. Generally, these investigations take place on purpose in controlled environments. But in 2018, a drilling incident caused a methane leak in the South China Sea . But what scientists including those at the University of Bremen, saw next shocked them more. Over the course of the next six years, in situ monitoring of the situation revealed an incredibly rapid response from the ecosystem. Within two years, the bacteria and worms had established a methane-munching 'worm bed' as per a study published in National Science Review.Cracks in the sea rocks allow methane to passively leak out into the ocean. But in 2018, gas hydrate exploration in the South China Sea caused a human-made underwater methane leak. They were trying to figure out how much natural gas might exist in marine sediments, so they drilled a 22-centimetre-wide hole in the deep seafloor. Afterwards, they tried to seal the hole with heavy mud. But their attempt failed.The incident wasn't detected until a year later, but it allowed researchers to study the seabed as the ecosystem quickly underwent a rapid and drastic transformation.A plume of methane gas had shot up from the deep, rising more than a kilometre high into the water column.Before the drilling event occurred, the seabed looked pretty much bare, with little in the way of benthic fauna making a living down there. Immediately following the leak, there was a further sharp decline in the seafloor life as microbial richness dipped by around 50 per cent.Between 2018 and 2023, the team, which included microbiologist Emil Ruff of the University of Bremen, tracked the ecosystem's development. They surveyed the site regularly using echo sounders, underwater cameras, chemical sensors, sediment samples and genetic analysis.Using echosounders, underwater cameras, and chemical sensors, researchers watched in awe as a swarm of ocean life flocked to the hole and contained the leaking gas with "remarkable speed". "Within just one to two years, an effective methane-consuming ecosystem had already formed," said microbial ecologist Emil Ruff of the University of Bremen in Germany as per a report by Sciencealert.com. According to past models, a fully functioning methane-munching community on the ocean floor can take between 60 and 100 years to develop. This one was chewing through nearly as much methane in a fraction of the time.Methane-munching bacteria underwater were having a gala time. The anaerobic methanotrophic archaea ANME-2e and ANME-3 had a bonanza, going from scarcely detectable to an expanding population. These microorganisms paved the way for bigger things to come. These single-celled organisms were then followed by an influx of burrowing invertebrates, which created an extensive 'worm bed' over the hole. Crustaceans crawled to the scene as well. Within 1 to 2 years, the once barren sediment was covered in an extensive “worm bed”. This was due to the rapid colonization by Spionid and Acrocirrid polychaete worms and Metridinid copepods."The worms, in turn, benefited from the newly established microorganisms, which likely served as a food source," explains Ruff. This crew of opportunistic invertebrates are thought to be a good indicator of early-stage seep ecosystems.The blooming of life – big and small – created a kind of animal-microbe biofilter that was breaking down methane about as effectively as methane seeps that had been going on for decades. Reaching 60 to 100 per cent of their methane-degrading capacity, they provided an ecosystem service that formed far quicker than previously thought possible.As tube worms burrowed into the seafloor, they helped mix the sediment, and this probably transported oxygen, nitrate, and sulfate into deeper layers, said Ruff.Bubbles of methane were still leaking from the hole in 2023, but as the living filter developed, the plume's height fell from 1,200 meters (0.74 miles) above the seafloor to roughly 800 meters.However, Ruff points out that the methane filter's rapid formation came at a cost: a marked change to the original ecosystem. Within a 20-meter (66-foot) radius, the diversity of bacteria and other microorganisms dropped by more than 50% within two years. Even 500 meters (1,640 feet) away, researchers detected elevated methane concentrations, along with a more than 30% drop in microbial diversity.The study, "Rapid de novo assembly of animal-microbe biofilter to mitigate seabed methane leakage," points to two parallel developments: The seafloor developed a strong capacity for methane breakdown in a short period of time, while the original biological community changed significantly in the process.
Article Summary: In 2018, a drilling incident caused a methane leak in the South China Sea. Over the course of the next six years, in situ monitoring of the situation revealed an incredibly rapid response from the ecosystem. Within two years, the bacteria and worms had established a methane-munching 'worm bed'

Article Title: Kansas student lost his class ring during a snowball fight with his future wife: 53 years later, when campus workers dug it out, the couple happened to be passing through the city
Article Text:
Pic credit: Lance Ziesch

The ring lost in the 1970s

Pic credit: Lance Ziesch

Campus workers unearth the ring

The heartfelt reunion

Pic credit: Lance Ziesch

Pic credit: Lance Ziesch

About the couple

Kansas student lost his class ring during a snowball fight with his future wife: 53 years later, when campus workers dug it out, the couple happened to be passing through the cityWhat are the odds of finding something lost for 53 years? Very slim. Now imagine it being discovered when its owner was driving through the same city, with the same person involved in the half-century-old incident, on the same stretch of highway. At some point, the coincidences start to feel almost impossible. And yet, that’s exactly what happened.Jim Burkhart lost his class ring to a snowball fight in 1973, while he was a student at Dodge City Community College (DC3). He wasn’t alone when he lost it. Marilyn Crockett was there, the woman he'd throw a snowball at with his left hand, the hand the ring sat on. She was there when it vanished into the Kansas dirt. Fifty-three years later, when the phone call came, she was there again, sitting next to him in the car, this time as his wife. The irrigation workers unearthed the ring while they were repairing the ground.This lost-and-found story gets so much better that, if you tried to pitch it as fiction, a filmmaker might send it back with a note: ‘Too many coincidences.The audience won’t buy it.’Jim Burkhart, a football player at DC3 in the early 1970s, lost the ring somewhere during the autumn of 1973. He was outside with Marilyn Crockett, the woman who would become his wife, and they were fooling around in the snow. Burkhart threw a snowball at her using his left hand, the same hand he wore his ring on. “I was feeling a little ornery… and I threw a snowball at her with my left hand,” Burkhart said, according to a news release by the college. He wore the ring on his left hand because of a childhood injury on his right. “She doesn’t remember if I hit her. I probably did. I had pretty good aim.”Whether or not the snowball reached the target, the ring surely flew off with the snowball. They searched the surrounding area. “We went back, looked a couple of times, and never did find the ring. And we would always kid about it. But yeah, we lost it that day,” he recalled. After the search turned up nothing, the couple moved on with their lives.Years passed by: more than half a century, to be precise. Burkhart went on with his life, and the ring remained submerged in layers of dirt. On August 7, Daemian Serna and Craig Mellecker, members of the DC3 grounds crew, were finishing up excavation work near the Administration Building when Serna spotted something shining in the soil. “I thought it was a gold hose clamp, which we don’t have. So, my interest was pretty piqued,” Serna said. But once he brushed the soil off, he realised it was a ring. “It said Kinsley High School. It had a little coyote on it and 1973. Then, I cleaned it a little more, and I saw two initials, one on each side, J and B. Craig right away looks over, and he goes, ‘Oh, somebody’s going to want that.’”After finishing their work, they called Kinsley High School. “Within an hour, he had a name and a story, and he got in contact with Jim right away,” Serna said. The find was quite rare for the workers, too. During their work, they stumble upon lots of things, but not something like this. “Usually, I just find old soda cans or trash in the dirt. Not an old high school ring from 50 years ago!”Burkhart and his wife, Marilyn Crockett, were driving to Tulsa that same day they got the call. In fact, they'd just visited Dodge City a week earlier, and during that visit, they'd talked once again about the missing ring. “You know, the ironic thing about the whole thing is, over the years, how many times we were in Dodge, and Marilyn would always bring up how we needed to go by the school and see if the ring was in the lost and found,” he said.Somewhere on the road, Burkhart's phone rang, with a woman on the other end asking if he'd lost a class ring on the college campus back in 1973. “I said, ‘Yeah, in 1973. I sure did.’ She said, ‘Well, they found it!’”For Serna, too, the whole incident was ‘kind of surreal’. “When we took him down to the quad, he went exactly where he remembered, and it was practically right there where we found it,” Serna said. “It’s really cool. It’s really movie-esque. It’s something you hear about in movies or on the news, not something you actually run into in real life!”Burkhart and Marilyn hadn't initially dated as high school classmates. They'd started seeing each other the summer after graduation, just before enrolling at DC3 together. He studied general studies and played football. She worked towards a secretarial certificate. After his football career ended, Burkhart transferred to Emporia State and had a career in education. The couple got married in 1976 while he was still a student. He worked in Kansas for 37 years, in different roles including teacher, coach, and administrator. His work took them to Meriden, Deerfield, Mulvane, and, ultimately, Goddard. Marilyn worked in secretarial positions at many of the same schools. They raised two daughters and eventually settled in Goddard. They have four grandchildren now.Over the years, the lost ring became a favourite story retold during Thanksgiving and family dinners. And just like that, life came full circle for Burkhart and his wife when the ring was found. Marilyn said she planned to take the ring to a jewellery store to have it cleaned up properly—a ring that had survived in the Kansas soil through seasons and years that neither of them would have predicted when that snowball went flying through the air. “I’m going to take it to them and say, ‘You’re not going to believe this!’” she said.
Article Summary: Jim Burkhart lost his class ring to a snowball fight in 1973, while he was a student at Dodge City Community College. The ring remained submerged in layers of dirt for more than half a century. Campus workers unearthed the ring while they were repairing the ground. When the phone call came, the woman who would become his wife was there.

Article Title: Six houses, Lamborghinis and dozens of Louis Vuitton bags: How a $250 million crypto fraud allegedly funded a luxury life
Article Text:
PC: FOX local, Orlando

Luxury life behind the $250 million crypto fraud

Delgado’s luxury purchases included Louis Vuitton bags

Image AI generated

How Goliath allegedly used investor money

Delgado pleads guilty to three federal charges

A $250 million crypto fraud allegedly financed a lavish lifestyle of luxury homes, Lamborghinis, Rolex watches and dozens of Louis Vuitton bags, according to the US Department of Justice. Christopher Alexander Delgado, former CEO of Goliath Ventures, pleaded guilty after admitting that his scheme caused at least $250 million in losses to investors. Prosecutors said investors were promised monthly returns from cryptocurrency “liquidity pools”, but their money was instead used to pay earlier investors, fund lavish travel and buy high-end assets. At least six residential properties were purchased, alongside luxury vehicles, watches and jewellery, as the alleged Ponzi scheme unravelled.According to the US Department of Justice, Goliath attracted investors with promises of monthly returns generated through cryptocurrency liquidity pools. The operation used personal referrals, professional marketing materials, luxury events, charitable sponsorships and some monthly payments presented as investment returns to build trust among investors. In reality, prosecutors said, the money was primarily used to return principal to those requesting it and for lavish spending.The scale of the spending was striking. According to the plea agreement and court documents, Delgado used investor funds to acquire at least six residential properties, with each property valued between $1.15 million and $8.5 million. The DOJ also said millions of dollars went to high-end vehicles, watches and jewellery, including Lamborghinis, Rolls-Royces and Rolex watches.The luxury purchases extended well beyond expensive cars and homes. Prosecutors said Delgado's spending included several dozen Louis Vuitton bags, wallets and pieces of luggage, alongside custom Tiffany jewellery. The collection of luxury goods became part of the assets that Delgado agreed to surrender as part of his guilty plea.The DOJ said Delgado has agreed to forfeit eight properties, 11 vehicles, 30 watches, more than 50 luxury bags and wallets, and 29 pieces of high-end jewellery. Cryptocurrency seized by the United States was included in the forfeiture agreement.The company presented itself to investors as an opportunity to earn returns from cryptocurrency liquidity pools. But the promised investment activity was not what most of the money went to. Instead, funds were used to pay purported returns to earlier investors and repay principal to investors who wanted their money back, while also funding business events, holidays, luxury travel and personal spending.The arrangement continued from at least January 2023 through January 2026. The DOJ described Goliath as a “Ponzi scheme”, in which purported returns for existing investors are paid using money contributed by newer investors. A companion civil asset forfeiture action identified at least $400 million paid by investors to Goliath, while Delgado admitted in his plea agreement that the scheme caused a minimum of $250 million in investor losses.US Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe said the spending was directly tied to the alleged fraud. “Delgado provided fraudulent information to solicit investor funds and then spent his ill-gotten gains on his extravagant lifestyle,” Kehoe stated. He added that his office would continue working with law enforcement partners to investigate fraud schemes and locate and seize assets linked to Delgado's scheme.Delgado pleaded guilty to three federal offences and faces a maximum of 20 years in prison for each fraud count and up to 10 years for the money laundering count. His sentencing hearing is scheduled for 8 October 2026. The case was investigated by IRS Criminal Investigation and Homeland Security Investigations, while the asset forfeiture proceedings are being handled separately.
Article Summary: Christopher Alexander Delgado, former CEO of Goliath Ventures, pleaded guilty after admitting that his scheme caused at least $250 million in losses to investors. Prosecutors said investors were promised monthly returns from cryptocurrency ‘liquidity pools’, but their money was instead used to pay earlier investors, fund lavish travel and buy high-end assets. At least six residential properties were purchased, alongside luxury vehicles, watches and jewellery, as the alleged Ponzi scheme unravelled.

Article Title: Miami flight overrun: Plane touched down at nearly 300 kmph despite high-speed warning
Article Text:
The flight data shows that the aircraft was still travelling at 158 knots, or about 293 kmph, when its nose and right main landing gear touched down.

What happened during the landing?

Pilots had noticed aircraft's speed

Aircraft issued multiple warnings

What the recorders tell investigators

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) has released preliminary findings into the runway overrun involving a 21 Air Boeing 767 at Miami International Airport. It revealed that the cargo plane touched down at nearly 300 kmph, despite a pilot warning that it was travelling too fast. The investigation also found that the crew attempted a go-around after touchdown, while there was no indication that the aircraft's speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.The findings come from the cockpit voice recorder (CVR) and flight data recorder (FDR) recovered from 21 Air Flight 7598. The Boeing 767-33A was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami when it overran the end of Runway 30 after landing.The flight data shows that the aircraft was still travelling at 158 knots, or about 293 kmph, when its nose and right main landing gear touched down.The brakes were applied shortly afterwards, when the aircraft was travelling at 146 knots, or about 270 kmph. The left main landing gear touched down when the speed had dropped to 134 knots, or about 248 kmph.This means the aircraft was already on the runway at a relatively high speed, leaving the crew with less distance to slow down before reaching the end.The NTSB's data shows that the brakes were then released when the aircraft was travelling at 120 knots.At that point, the engines were briefly powered up in a manner consistent with an attempt to go around.The report says the throttles were then brought back to idle and the brakes were applied again. The aircraft was travelling at 117 knots at that stage.The cockpit recording suggests that speed had been a concern even before the aircraft touched down.During the approach, one pilot called for the flaps to be set to 20 degrees. The other pilot responded that they were travelling too fast.The pilot continued making comments about the aircraft's excessive speed during the remainder of the recording. The NTSB said there was no consistent verbal response to those comments.The report records the sequence as follows:"A pilot called for ﬂaps to be set to 20 degrees, and the other pilot cautioned they were too fast. The other pilot made additional comments regarding the aircr​aft’s excessive speed throughout the remainder of the recording. There was not a consistent verbal response to the comments about speed."The autopilot then appears to have been disconnected about 1 minute and 23 seconds before the end of the CVR recording.The aircraft also received several automated warnings as it approached the runway.The system issued a "sink rate sink rate" warning, followed by a "too low terrain" warning. The latter warning was repeated four times during the approach.The NTSB's preliminary timeline records:"Electronic “sink rate sink rate” callout."It later records:"Electronic “too low terrain” callout. Annunciated four times."Another "too low terrain" warning was recorded later during the approach.These warnings indicate that the aircraft's approach was generating alerts from its onboard warning systems as it descended towards the runway.Go-around was called, but aircraft had already landedThe cockpit recording shows that a pilot called for a go-around about 15 seconds after sounds consistent with the aircraft touching down.The FDR data also shows that the throttles were briefly increased to a setting consistent with go-around thrust.However, the engines were then brought back to idle and the brakes were applied again.The NTSB's data shows that there was no indication of the aircraft using its speed brakes or thrust reversers.In simple terms, the aircraft had landed, the crew attempted to initiate a go-around, but the aircraft then returned to idle engine power and braking was reapplied as it continued along the runway.The aircraft's recorded speed fell to 96 knots before the flight data recorder showed marked changes in its lateral, longitudinal and vertical acceleration.The final recorded groundspeed was 65 knots.The NTSB recovered both recorders from the accident site and successfully read them at its Vehicle Recorder Laboratory in Washington DC.The cockpit voice recorder contained more than two hours of good-quality audio across four channels. The flight data recorder contained about 54 hours of information and recorded more than 400 parameters.Investigators will now conduct a more detailed review of the cockpit recording and prepare a written transcript.The NTSB stressed that the findings released on September 9 are preliminary and could change as the investigation continues.The current data, however, provides a clearer picture of the final moments: the aircraft approached and landed at high speed, the crew had raised concerns about speed, multiple automated warnings were heard, a go-around was called after touchdown, and there was no recorded indication that speed brakes or thrust reversers were deployed.
Article Summary: 21 Air Boeing 767-33A was flying from San Juan, Puerto Rico, to Miami when it overran the end of Runway 30 after landing. The flight data shows that the aircraft was still travelling at 158 knots, or about 293 kmph, when its nose and right main landing gear touched down. There was no indication of the aircraft using its speed brakes or thrust reversers. The aircraft's recorded speed fell to 96 knots before the flight data recorder showed marked changes.

Article Title: Around 1,700 passengers boarded a Royal Caribbean Alaska cruise and waited on the ship in Vancouver; two days later, the entire sailing was canceled
Article Text:
The company didn’t offer any information about what the technical issue entailed

Why the cruise was cancelled

Passengers scramble to change their plans

Refunds and future cruise credit offered

Around 1,700 passengers who had boarded Royal Caribbean’s Serenade of the Seas in Vancouver for an Alaska cruise were left without a voyage after the entire sailing was cancelled because of ongoing maintenance work. The passengers had already spent time on the ship when they were told that the cruise would not go ahead.The seven-night Alaska cruise was originally scheduled to leave Vancouver on August 30, People's magazine reported. About a week before the planned departure, passengers were informed that the cruise would instead be shortened to five nights. The departure was also moved to September 1.Passengers were still invited to board the ship on September 1 and use it as a hotel while they waited for the vessel to leave Vancouver. About 1,700 passengers boarded, expecting the delayed cruise to eventually begin. However, the departure time passed without the ship leaving the port.Passengers were told that the departure had been delayed, but an announcement later informed them that Royal Caribbean had cancelled the entire sailing. Guests were given until midnight the following day to leave the ship, turning what had been planned as the beginning of an Alaska holiday into an unexpected scramble to make new travel arrangements.Royal Caribbean said the cancellation was linked to ongoing maintenance work on Serenade of the Seas. The cruise line did not provide details about the specific technical issue involved.“To accommodate ongoing maintenance, we’ve had to cancel our sailing,” a Royal Caribbean spokesperson told USA Today and Fox News. “We apologize to our guests for the inconvenience and have worked with them to adjust their travel plans.”The company had first told passengers about the maintenance issue before the original August 30 departure date. At that stage, the seven-night cruise was changed to a five-night sailing, while the departure was pushed back to September 1.Passengers were allowed to spend time on the ship while it remained in Vancouver. They could use much of the vessel and could also leave to explore the city. Some areas, including the casino, remained closed.Arielle Anderson, a 28-year-old mother and lawyer from South Carolina, had booked the cruise as a gift for her family. She told USA Today that they had “been looking forward to this since Christmas.”The family had wanted to visit Alaska and had already travelled for the planned holiday. After the cruise was initially shortened, Anderson said cancelling the trip and getting refunds for their tickets would have been difficult because members of the family were flying in from different parts of the country.Instead, the family travelled to Whistler before boarding the ship on September 1.Anderson said passengers were instructed to board the vessel as part of the immigration process. Once on board, they waited for the ship to depart, but the expected departure time passed. Later, they were told that the departure had been delayed.By the evening, passengers were informed that the entire cruise had been cancelled. Anderson described the reaction among guests as chaotic.“Everybody was kind of panicking, so we were all just sitting in one of the bar areas, and everybody was just on their phones,” Anderson said. “People were really upset because everybody was trying to find flights and hotels and stuff.”Royal Caribbean offered passengers affected by the cancellation a full refund. According to USA Today, the company also offered a 100% future cruise credit for the fare and reimbursement for flight change fees.Passengers were also set to receive a pro-rated refund for dining and beverage packages, according to the New York Post.For Anderson’s family, the cancelled cruise meant changing the holiday rather than ending it completely. Her mother found a rental car, and the family travelled to a vacation rental near Bellingham, Washington, while keeping their original flight home from Vancouver.“We just got an Airbnb down here, and have just been hanging out around here, hiking and whatnot,” Anderson said. “Definitely not what we planned, but [we’re] trying to make the best of it.”The cancellation also left other passengers wondering what would happen to later sailings involving the ship. Some raised questions on cruise message boards about future trips that had already been booked.According to CruiseMapper, Serenade of the Seas later departed Vancouver for another Alaska cruise on September 6.
Article Summary: Royal Caribbean said the cancellation was linked to ongoing maintenance work on Serenade of the Seas. The cruise line did not provide details about the specific technical issue involved. Royal Caribbean offered passengers affected by the cancellation a full refund and a 100% future cruise credit.

Article Title: Netherlands built a 9-km storm barrier to protect against floods; decades later, “sand hunger” began shrinking tidal flats
Article Text:
Image: Wikipedia

The Eastern Scheldt Barrier was built after the 1953 flood

The barrier changed how sand moved through the estuary

North-eastern section of Oosterscheldekering (Image: Wikipedia)

Tidal flats began disappearing as sand was carried away

The Netherlands is now adding sand to restore the lost habitat

The Netherlands built one of the world’s most ambitious flood defences after the devastating North Sea flood of 1953. Completed in 1986, the 9-kilometre Eastern Scheldt Barrier was designed to protect hundreds of thousands of people while keeping the estuary open to tides and saltwater. But the engineering solution created an unexpected environmental consequence. By reducing tidal currents, the barrier disrupted the natural movement of sand across the Eastern Scheldt. Decades later, tidal flats and shoals are steadily shrinking in a process known as “sand hunger”.The Eastern Scheldt Barrier was built as part of the Netherlands’ Delta Works, the huge national programme created after the catastrophic North Sea flood of 1953. Construction began in 1976 and took 10 years to complete. According to Rijkswaterstaat Ministry of Infrastructure and Water Management, the barrier stretches 9 kilometres between Schouwen-Duiveland and Noord-Beveland in Zeeland, with 3 kilometres containing movable floodgates. Unlike a conventional dam, it normally remains open so that tides can continue flowing through the Eastern Scheldt. The decision preserved the estuary’s natural environment and helped protect the region’s fishing industry while providing a powerful defence against exceptionally high water.Keeping the Eastern Scheldt open preserved tidal exchange, but it did not leave the estuary’s natural processes unchanged. The official data explains that the barrier reduced the volume of tidal water moving through the system, weakening the currents that previously transported sediment. As a result, less sand returns to the tidal flats, mudflats and salt marshes during the ebb-and-flow cycle. A report, ‘ Oosterschelde Storm Surge Barrier: development of scour pits and stability of seabed protection ’, by Rijkswaterstaat Waterdienst researchers from Deltares found that the morphological situation after construction was no longer in equilibrium, with the remaining channels becoming relatively too large while tidal-flat and mudflat areas experienced erosion. This sediment shortage became known as “sand hunger”.The consequences are particularly visible on the exposed tidal landscapes of the Eastern Scheldt. During storms, large quantities of sand can move from the flats and mudflats into deeper channels, while the weaker tidal currents are unable to return enough sediment. These areas are therefore becoming progressively smaller. Its 2012 morphological report recorded average erosion of roughly 1 centimetre per year on the Eastern Scheldt’s tidal flats and mudflats. Rising sea levels add another long-term pressure. Without intervention, the shrinking areas could gradually disappear beneath the water, reducing important habitat for wildlife and changing the shape of the estuary.Rijkswaterstaat is responding by deliberately putting sand back onto vulnerable areas. A current project at the Galgeplaat tidal flat and the Slikken van den Dortsman is scheduled to run from 2022 to 2027, with sand nourishment taking place during 2026 and 2027. The aim is to keep these landscapes above water for longer and maintain their ecological functions. The tidal flats provide feeding grounds for wading and migratory birds, while seals use them as resting places. The Slikken van den Dortsman also helps reduce wave energy before it reaches nearby dikes. After the nourishment work, there are plans to monitor the results for at least five years.The Eastern Scheldt Barrier therefore illustrates an unusual challenge in environmental engineering, solving one problem can create another. The structure remains a crucial part of Dutch flood protection, but by altering tidal currents, it also changed the sediment balance that maintained the estuary’s shallow landscapes. Now, decades after the barrier was completed, the Netherlands is using carefully placed sand to compensate for that change and keep the Eastern Scheldt’s tidal flats, wildlife habitat and coastal defences functioning.
Article Summary: The Eastern Scheldt Barrier was built after the 1953 North Sea flood. It was designed to protect hundreds of thousands of people while keeping the estuary open to tides and saltwater. But the engineering solution created an unexpected environmental consequence. By reducing tidal currents, the barrier disrupted the natural movement of sand. Decades later, tidal flats and shoals are shrinking in a process known as ‘sand hunger’ The Netherlands is now adding sand to restore the lost habitat.

Article Title: 'Not invited': Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman on Brics Summit in Delhi
Article Text:
India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam

Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will not attend the Brics Summit in New Delhi after Dhaka said he was not invited to the two-day meeting.Bangladesh state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said on Thursday there was scope for the country to send a government representative to the summit, but ruled out Tarique Rahman’s participation.“How shall we go? Has anyone from the Bangladesh government been invited? Our prime minister was not invited. Who told you that our Prime Minister was invited? The BIMSTEC Chair was invited. Then why are you asking this question?” he told reporters at the Foreign Service Academy, according to The Daily Star.Kobir said the invitation had been extended to the chair of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), rather than Bangladesh’s prime minister.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam. The summit is being held under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.The meeting is expected to bring several international leaders and high-level delegations to the national capital.Ahead of the summit, Delhi Police has stepped up security across the city, with around 15,000 personnel and nearly 200 companies of paramilitary forces deployed for the event.“Police have been deployed in different sector zones across New Delhi. Drills have been conducted. CCTVs are being monitored. Meetings have been held with agencies... Our technical equipment has been installed so that any threat can be detected. We are ensuring that the public does not face any kind of inconvenience,” Sharma said.
Article Summary: India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam. Delhi Police has stepped up security across the city, with around 15,000 personnel and nearly 200 companies of paramilitary forces deployed for the event.

Article Title: Trump's top advisors warn him Iran war could drag through end of his term: Report
Article Text:
Trump launched the conflict as an effort to pressure Iran over its nuclear programme.

Trump expects 'a quick end'

US-Iran fighting continues

Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency, despite his public prediction that the conflict will end soon after this year’s midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were among the advisers who reportedly raised the possibility during private discussions with Trump in the Oval Office and Situation Room.According to the report, the officials told Trump that Iran could continue resisting US pressure, potentially keeping the conflict going until after the next US presidential inauguration in January 2029.Trump has publicly offered a much shorter timeline for the conflict. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, he said he expected the war to end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November. He argued that Iran was attempting to influence the election but would not be able to maintain its resistance for much longer."I think the war will end immediately after the election... They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we could get a nice, weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon."Trump has also indicated that diplomatic talks remain possible, although he has said negotiations are not his preferred option.Trump also referred to recent US strikes on Iran and attacks involving Iranian and American forces."We've knocked out nine of their ships; I would say that the attacks are caused by us — and you're going to see a lot more. We've taken our about nine of their tankers. Many of them are gone-zo."The US launched strikes on Iranian oil tankers during its latest offensive after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted US naval warships earlier this week.Iran has also retaliated, with multiple explosions reported over an American airbase in Jordan.Trump launched the conflict as an effort to pressure Iran over its nuclear programme. The first US strikes were carried out on February 28 as part of Operation Epic Fury, in coordination with Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The opening strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, according to the material provided.The reported warning from Trump's senior advisers highlights the gap between the administration's private assessment of a potentially prolonged conflict and Trump's public expectation of a rapid end.
Article Summary: Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly raised the possibility during private discussions with Trump in the Oval Office and Situation Room. According to the report, the officials told Trump that Iran could keep resisting US pressure, potentially keeping the conflict going until after the next US presidential inauguration in January 2029.

Article Title: From voter ID to $5,000 cheques: Trump goes desi, mimics India’s election toolkit
Article Text:
Trump’s $5,000 dividend promise and push for voter ID suggest he is borrowing from India’s playbook of direct welfare and voter identification as electoral tools.

$5,000

Trump dividend

Trump cash push comes amid mounting US national debt which surpassed $40tn in August

US national debt has soared under Trump’s second administration.

From welfare to political technology

ID first, benefits later

Trump mid August had praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act

A president under pressure

US President Donald Trump may never admit it, but it’s self-evident. The self-proclaimed oldest democracy is beginning to borrow from political toolkit of the world’s largest democracy.It first reflected in Trump’s obsession with photo identification for voting. Now comes the promise of money.It’s scene which is quite familiar for Indians. Come election time and it starts raining freebies for voters. The template works like this: Make promises first and then do economic calculations later, once you have won the polls.Now, something similar is happening in US.At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump offered voters a strikingly transactional proposition: Return Republicans to power in Congress and every adult American citizen could receive $5,000.“Pretend that I’m on the ballot just one more time,” Trump told supporters.“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate...I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said.“It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. “Now all we have to do is win.”With potentially more than 200 million payments, Trump could be promising well over $1 trillion in “dividends” unless the programme is restricted by income or other eligibility criteria, a WSJ report said.There is little chance that a $1 trillion-plus payout would sail through Congress at a moment when US public debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time and is already pushing up borrowing costs.But as political messaging, the promise matters. For anyone familiar with Indian elections, the formula feels instantly recognisable.Make voter identity a major political issue. Build databases capable of identifying citizens and beneficiaries. Deliver welfare directly rather than through opaque bureaucracies. Brand the benefit aggressively. And, most importantly, make sure the voter knows exactly which government put the money in the account.Trump, in other words, appears to be discovering the politics of Indian-style direct welfare.India’s welfare state has changed dramatically over the past decade. The Modi government’s Direct Benefit Transfer(DBT) changed that relationship.Money began arriving straight into bank accounts. A voter receiving Rs 2,000 directly into a bank account does not need a politician to explain government policy. That is electoral gold.Indian states took the idea further.Cash assistance for girls and women has become one of the most powerful electoral instruments in recent times.Madhya Pradesh’s Ladli Behna programme, Maharashtra’s Ladki Bahin scheme and similar initiatives elsewhere turned women not merely into welfare recipients but into a distinct political constituency.Indian politicians have understood that modern welfare is not merely about how much governments spend. It is about how clearly citizens can identify the sender.That is the political insight hiding inside Trump’s $5,000 proposal.However, Tump's dividend is not identical to India's DBT schemes: It targets no specific demographic and depends on a Congress that shows no appetite for it. But the underlying instinct is the same one Indian incumbents have refined: Convert a government or leader's flagging popularity into a direct, personal payment timed to the ballot box, and let voters decide whether to reward the giver.The other Indian parallel is Trump’s push for tougher voter identification. In his March 2025 executive order overhauling federal election procedures, Trump explicitly cited India and Brazil for linking voter identity to biometric databases, contrasting them with an American system that leans on self-attestation of citizenship.In August, Trump again posted on Truth Social about photo ID cards."We need to pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT, now!" Trump wrote, invoking legislation that would mandate citizenship proof and government-issued photo ID for federal voting.His administration has repeatedly argued that US elections require stronger proof of identity and citizenship.However, India’s system is more complicated than that comparison suggests.The Electors Photo Identity Card, or EPIC, is widely used, but it is not the sole document voters can present. The Election Commission accepts several alternative photo identification documents, and Aadhaar is not mandatory for voting.The US also does not start from zero. Most states already have some form of voter identification requirement.Still, politically, Trump is assembling two ideas that sit comfortably together in the Indian political imagination: Prove who the voter is and then deliver benefits directly to that person.Trump has promised to campaign aggressively for Republicans and he is expected to make about 35 trips on behalf of candidates in closely fought races. He is also directing his political action committee to deploy some of the hundreds of millions of dollars it has raised in key contests, a Bloomberg report said.There is no doubt that Trump is feeling the heat. Polling shows Americans unconvinced by Trump's insistence that affordability complaints are overblown, and Wednesday's convention drew visible empty seats as vulnerable Republican candidates skipped the event altogether.Trump’s popularity is at all-time low and he has entangled US in what seems to be a forever war with Iran.But politically, the message is unmistakable. Faced with the prospect of losing Congress and spending the remainder of his presidency as a lame duck, Trump appears increasingly willing to borrow from India’s electoral playbook.
Article Summary: Donald Trump is borrowing from India's playbook of direct welfare and voter ID as electoral tools. At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump offered voters a strikingly transactional proposition: Return Republicans to power in Congress and every adult American citizen could receive $5,000.

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director and daughter of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , has resigned from her post following fraud investigations by the UN agency and Bangladeshi authorities, Reuters reported on Wednesday.Wazed’s resignation was confirmed in a resignation letter seen by Reuters. Article Title: 'Make ground in Gaza tremble': Egypt warned Netanyahu of Hamas plans before October 7
Article Text:
Details emerge on Egypt’s warning to Netanyahu

Fresh details have emerged about warnings issued to Israel ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, amid a report that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by the United Arab Emirates about plans for a major assault in the weeks leading up to the invasion.The latest information also sheds further light on previously reported warnings from Egyptian intelligence officials during the same period.According to Army Radio, the Shin Bet intelligence service conveyed to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warnings from its Egyptian counterparts that Hamas intended to “make the ground in Gaza tremble.”The Egyptian side provided only a general warning, without offering any specific details.In the days following the October 7 onslaught, an Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning “something big,” including an apparent direct warning from Cairo’s intelligence minister to Netanyahu, as cited by Times of Israel.According to the report, then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar assessed that the warning referred, at least in part, to Hamas seeking to raise the issue of kidnapped Israeli researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in talks with Israel over a potential hostage deal.Shortly before the warning was issued, Hamas and Iraqi Shiite militia Kataeb Hezbollah, the group holding Tsurkov, had reportedly agreed that she would be treated as a Hamas asset in negotiations with Israel.The talks would involve the release of a large number of terrorists in exchange for the handover of two Israeli captives and the bodies of two IDF soldiers held in Gaza.The development comes as a new investigative report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claimed that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a “major attack” against Israel. Netanyahu, however, reportedly did not share the warning with Israel’s senior security leadership.Around 10 days after their reported conversation, Hamas launched its October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.The Haaretz report is based on the new book Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment, which claims that bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu for 45 minutes from Abu Dhabi. During the conversation, bin Zayed also reportedly urged Netanyahu to address broader sources of instability, including Gaza’s economic situation and rising tensions in the West Bank.According to a UAE presidential adviser interviewed for the book, bin Zayed was “surprised” by Netanyahu’s response, saying the Israeli prime minister did not appear “alarmed”.However, Netanyahu's office has rejected the claims made by the report.In a post on X, the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said that any exchange of relevant information between the two countries took place solely through intelligence channels.“The press reports are false. No warning was given to the Prime Minister by the United Arab Emirates before October 7. If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries,” it posted.
Article Summary: Details emerge about warnings issued to Israel ahead of October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. Israel's Shin Bet intelligence service warned that Hamas intended to ‘make the ground in Gaza tremble’ Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning ‘something big’

Article Title: In 2016, US dairy farmers dumped 43 million gallons of milk, the largest recorded loss in at least 16 years, as production outran the plants able to process it
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image: A dairy tanker is shown releasing surplus milk at a farm facility, illustrating the large-scale milk disposal that occurred when US production outpaced available processing capacity. Credits: ChatGPT

How a 2014 price increase fed the later glut

When the surplus reached the processing system

Representative image of a cow powered farm. Credits: Wikimedia Commons

Why lower farm prices did not mean equally cheap milk in the market

In the first eight months of 2016, US dairy producers and handlers discarded, dumped, or lost more than 43 million gallons of milk. The US Department of Agriculture’s data suggest that the volume was the largest amount of milk wasted in at least 16 years of comparable information. Some of the discarded or dumped milk went into fields, manure lagoons or animal feed. Meanwhile, some was lost along truck routes or discarded at processing plants. The Wall Street Journal report said the amount was equivalent to about 66 Olympic-size swimming pools.As raw milk is perishable, it cannot be stored indefinitely while producers wait for prices or demand to improve. Concurrently, dairy processors were dealing with large inventories of products like cheese. This resulted in a bottleneck in which some milk had little practical or economic destination, driven by the unceasing daily output of herds managed on continuous, year-round calving and lactation schedules.The imbalance was no sudden change. Instead, it had been building for more than a year. In September 2014, the US all-milk price reached $25.70 per hundredweight, which is equal to 100 pounds of milk.High prices encouraged dairy farmers to expand production, and US milk output subsequently rose to 208.6 billion pounds in 2015. This was 1.2% above 2014. Market analysts explained that dairy production responds slowly to changing prices because expanding or reducing herds takes time.The production response continued even after the prices began falling. By April 2016, the all-milk price had dropped to $15 per hundredweight, which had fallen sharply from the peak in 2014. Yet in June 2016, the USDA forecasted that annual output would refuse to bend, holding steady at a projected 212.6 billion pounds. Industry tracking noted that farmers could reduce some costs or remove less productive cows. Though, many costs associated with maintaining a dairy herd could not be avoided simply by cutting production.Another reason why output remained high was that the production costs were relatively favourable. The agency’s later review of 2016 found that feed prices had fallen during late 2015 and remained low through most of 2016. Milk production per cow also increased, and by the end of the year, the country had produced a record 212.5 billion pounds of milk, 1.7% more than in 2015. The average milk production per cow rose by 1.4%.The challenge, therefore, was that production was responding with a lag to the favourable economics of the earlier period, while the international market had changed considerably. Several federal reports suggest that global demand for dairy products was relatively weak, particularly in China, while the US dollar remained strong. Several major producing countries had also redirected European dairy products toward markets where US exporters competed due to Russia’s ban on most dairy imports. In addition to that, the European Union ended its milk supply quotas in April 2015, after which EU milk production increased and added to global supplies.While the dairy products are traded globally, the effects eventually appeared inside the US supply chain. The government agency reported that exports of some major dairy products weakened between 2014 and 2015, while imports increased. Cheese exports fell by 114 million pounds, or 14%, and dry-whey exports declined by 106 million pounds, or 22%. At the same time, imports of cheese and butter increased, leaving milk and dairy products competing for domestic processing, storage and sales channels.On the other hand, for farmers and milk handlers, converting surplus raw milk into another dairy product was not always an immediate solution. Contemporary reporting noted that some producers could find themselves better off disposing of milk than moving it to a processor when the economics of transportation and processing stopped working. Therefore, the industry started exploring different ways to absorb milk through existing consumer markets. Dairy Management Inc. worked with food companies and restaurant chains to increase the amount of dairy ingredients used in products. Although these measures could increase demand, they were incremental responses to a much bigger imbalance in production and inventories.The collapse in farm prices was substantial, but consumers did not experience the same percentage decline at stores. USDA reported that prices received by dairy farmers fell about 40% between September 2014 and April 2016. Over approximately the same period, the retail price of whole milk fell 16%, from $3.77 per gallon in October 2014 to $3.16 in April 2016.By the end of 2016, the industry’s financial picture remained difficult despite the record production. The annual average all-milk price fell to $16.24 per hundredweight from $17.12 in 2015. While prices staged a modest late-season rally to reach an average of $17.67 per hundredweight in the fourth quarter, the annual figure still heavily reflected the impact of the earlier collapse. The government agency attributed the relatively low 2016 prices to the combination of abundant global supplies, relatively slow demand growth in some markets, continued Russian trade restrictions and stronger European competition, along with the strong US dollar.
Article Summary: In the first eight months of 2016, US dairy producers and handlers discarded, dumped, or lost more than 43 million gallons of milk. Some of the discarded or dumped milk went into fields, manure lagoons or animal feed. Meanwhile, some was lost along truck routes or discarded at processing plants. The amount was equivalent to about 66 Olympic-size swimming pools.

Article Title: In 2018, Burberry disclosed destroying £28.6 million of unsold clothing, perfume and accessories; the company said the practice helped protect brand exclusivity
Article Text:
Burberry's store in Oslo, Norway. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The £28.6 million figure covered the year ending March 31, 2018

The company said the goal was protecting brand exclusivity, not simply managing waste

Shareholder and lawmaker scrutiny followed almost immediately

Fixing Fashion

Burberry reversed the policy by September 2018

Disposable textile waste. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

In 2018, Burberry disclosed in its annual report that it had physically destroyed £28.6 million worth of unsold clothing, perfume, and accessories over the previous financial year, a routine practice in luxury retail that became a public controversy as soon as the figure came to light. The disclosure, buried in a lengthy annual filing, drew immediate scrutiny from the media, shareholders and lawmakers, and the company announced in September 2018 that it would stop destroying unsold merchandise except as a last resort.Burberry's annual report stated that the cost of finished goods physically destroyed that year came to £28.6 million, a figure later cited directly in a UK House of Commons Environmental Audit Committee report examining sustainability across the fashion industry. This was an increase from £26.9 million in the previous year, according to Burberry’s 2017/18 annual report. Among the products destroyed were clothes, accessories and perfume that had not been sold through regular distribution channels. The company chose to burn off the products instead of selling them at a reduced price or donating them away. This, as stated by the company, helped them capture the energy that was released during the process.According to Burberry, the new policy was designed to prevent any surplus from entering the grey market. The grey market is characterized by discount items that may erode a brand’s premium positioning. By selling the surplus goods at a discount, Burberry said that it could diminish the value of its brand as well as create an opportunity for counterfeiters, because counterfeit products may benefit from discounted goods for legitimacy. The justification provided by Burberry was not uncommon within the fashion retail industry. The committee noted that the Burberry stock-burning case had drawn attention to wider concerns about how fashion companies handled unsold goods.Thereport said that “the fashion industry has marked its own homework for too long” and called for stronger government action, including mandatory due diligence and measures to make retailers take greater responsibility for textile waste. The Fixing Fashion report itself cites data showing only 55% of the 150 brands and retailers surveyed by Fashion Revolution's 2018 Transparency Index were publishing measurable, time-bound environmental goals, with just 6% offering repair services. Advocacy groups added to the pressure. The parliamentary committee's findings highlighted the wider problem of unsold stock and called for stronger government action on textile waste.As per a statement issued by Burberry in September 2018, the company stated that in future, Burberry will stop the practice of destroying unsold merchandise and will opt for reusing, repairing, donating, or recycling unsold products as far as possible, destroying them only as a last resort when products are defective, damaged, or obsolete, a carve-out critics noted could still cover much of the unsold seasonal stock the original practice was meant to address. However, legislators in the committee report acknowledged the commitment but claimed that other firms in the industry had failed to do so. In that same September 2018 statement, Burberry separately announced, as an unrelated policy shift, that it would stop using real fur in its products.A recommendation made by the Environmental Audit Committee in their Fixing Fashion report of February 2019 suggested that the British government should stop the practice of burning and burying unsold stocks of clothes that can be recycled and reused. The recommendations did not become laws, but the findings of the committee were largely based on the attention that was garnered by Burberry's disclosure and it was used as an exemplary case where voluntary commitments alone were perceived as insufficient. It was hard to tell whether other British firms were disposing of as many items as Burberry, yet most companies give very little information on the issue as compared to Burberry in their annual reports.
Article Summary: In 2018, Burberry disclosed in its annual report that it had physically destroyed £28.6 million worth of unsold clothing, perfume, and accessories over the previous financial year. The disclosure drew immediate scrutiny from the media, shareholders and lawmakers. The company announced in September 2018 that it would stop destroying unsold merchandise except as a last resort.

Complete baggage checks for explosives and the items that were once allowed banned such as small knives, razor blades, scissors, and box cutter because of the potential use as a weapon.Initially all liquids, including beverages and hygiene, were prohibited, and for this reason, carrying full-sized toiletries, fragrances, and larger water bottles were also not allowed.1. Article Title: In the 1950s, Florida landscapers introduced an Asian ornamental tree; decades later, soapberry bugs feeding on it had beaks about 30% shorter than those on native balloon vine
Article Text:
Chinese golden rain tree, fruit or seed pods. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A 1992 study first documented the beak-length divergence between host populations

Beak reduction accompanied broader shifts in the bugs' development and survival

A 2016 follow-up study found the native-adapted ecotype had largely disappeared

Soapberry Bugs Subfamily Serinethinae. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

It was in the 1950s that Florida landscape gardeners planted the golden rain tree (Koelreuteria elegans), a non-native ornamental from Taiwan with yellow flowers and light, papery seed pods, as the UF/IFAS Assessment of Non-Native Plants and other sources on the species confirm. In what can be termed an immediate attraction to the non-native plant, the soapberry bug, which is an insect that uses its long, sharp beak to penetrate plants in search of food, started using the newly introduced tree for food. As stated in Living on Earth, the length of the beak for the bugs eating from the golden rain tree had become significantly reduced, becoming nearly 30 percent shorter than the beak of bugs eating the native balloon vine within the course of only 50 years.The basis for the experiment was established in the paper 'Host Race Radiation in the Soapberry Bug: Natural History with the History,' which appeared in Evolution in 1992, written by Scott P. Carroll and Christin Boyd. In the study, the authors took a closer look at these Florida populations, using both museum material and current sampling.They found that beak length was associated with the change of the host plant over time, with insects feeding on the native balloon vine having longer beaks, and those feeding on the introduced golden rain tree having shorter, seed-piercing beaks. To ensure the fact that it was not a pre-existing condition but a recently acquired one, Carroll and Boyd made comparisons between the current populations and the museum specimens collected before the introduction of the new host plant.The insects adapting to the golden rain tree showed more changes than just the reduced length of their mouthparts. Another observation made in the 1992 study is that variations were observed in development time and survival rate based on the host plant from which a particular population of bugs fed, indicating that variation in beak size was just one of several adaptations Carroll and Boyd documented. The later study conducted by Carroll et al. took these discoveries further and showed some genetically-based differences in performance when comparing insects from their native host with those from another host. With the golden rain tree producing abundant amounts of seeds on all trees grown across suburban and urban Florida, the adaptation of the bugs to this abundant and accessible host provided a good example for studying the evolution process.However, in 2016, a second study titled 'Adaptation to an invasive host is driving the loss of a native ecotype' was published by Meredith Cenzer in the journal Evolution , which sought to test how well the local adaptation pattern persisted in these same Florida populations. Cenzer combined field surveys with morphology and host-use data and found that bugs were still present on the native balloon vine, but their phenotypes had converged with those of the invasive-host population: the distinct, long-beaked native-adapted ecotype was essentially gone, replaced by populations that were now better adapted to the golden rain tree across the board, likely through gene flow from the invasive-host populations.The mechanism behind this may be gene flow. Bugs adapted to the golden rain tree may have hybridized with balloon vine populations enough to reduce the prevalence of genes associated with the long-beaked form, regardless of whether balloon vine disappeared from the environment. However, more recent research on this system indicates that maladaptive plasticity also contributed to the development of this scenario, suggesting that gene flow alone is not the only explanation. Together, the two studies show how quickly evolutionary patterns can shift and then reverseTogether, the two studies serve as an example of how quickly natural selection can drive a significant physical change, and of how quickly that change can be undone by gene flow rather than by a genuine reversal. While the earlier study traced the evolution of differences in beak length within just a few decades of the golden rain tree's introduction, the later study found that the short-beaked, invasive-adapted form had instead spread through the whole regional population, swamping and erasing the longer-beaked native-adapted ecotype rather than the population reverting to it. As far as evolutionary biology is concerned, the soapberry bug example can serve as a good one for consideration since it demonstrates both aspects of evolution in a rather easy-to-follow system.
Article Summary: A 1992 study first documented the beak-length divergence between host populations. A 2016 follow-up study found the native-adapted ecotype had largely disappeared. Bugs adapted to the golden rain tree may have hybridized with balloon vine populations to reduce the prevalence of genes associated with the long-beaked form.

Article Title: Before 9/11, US knew Bin Laden was a threat. India-Pakistan tensions were the bigger worry
Article Text:
The towers of the World Trade Center pour smoke shortly after being struck by hijacked commercial aircraft, September 11, 2001. (Image source: Reuters)

India and Pakistan

The problem next door

Osama bin Laden (File photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe that the United States paid enough attention to the threat of Osama bin Laden before 9/11? Yes, they were aware and took sufficient action No, they underestimated the threat 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

When terrorism became a secondary problem

Washington knew about Bin Laden

9/11 has been one of the most horrifying incidents of terrorism to happen on American soil. It claimed 2,977 victims not even accounting for the collective trauma it resulted in.By the time four hijacked planes tore through the American skies, Washington had already spent years watching the rise of Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda.The problem, as the 9/11 Commission Report makes clear that, in South Asia, American attention was repeatedly pulled towards another crisis.The Commission report makes it a point to highlight that: "In the State Department, concerns about India-Pakistan tensions often crowded out attention to Afghanistan or Bin Ladin. Aware of instability and growing Islamic extremism in Pakistan, State Department officials worried most about an arms race and possible war between Pakistan and India."Washington knew Pakistan was unstable and it also knew that Islamist extremism was growing there. They also had information that Pakistan supported the Taliban and were aware of Bin Laden operating from within Afghanistan.But the possibility of an arms race, and eventually war, between two nuclear-armed neighbours kept competing for the top spot on the American agenda.After India and Pakistan conducted nuclear tests in May 1998, that competition became even harder to ignore.The Commission says the dangers of an arms race and possible war became “daily first-order concerns” for State Department officials.Bin Laden was meanwhile building something else.In February 1998, he publicly declared that killing Americans was an individual duty for Muslims who could do so. Three months later, in an interview with ABC, he warned that if what he described as American “injustice” continued, the battle would eventually move to American soil. The Commission notes that plans to attack the United States had been developing with “unwavering single-mindedness” throughout the 1990s.For the United States, getting to Bin Laden meant dealing with Pakistan. The report also acknowledges that Bin Laden was well-known and a senior figure among Islamist extremists, especially those in Egypt, the Arabian Peninsula, and the Afghanistan-Pakistan border region. Yet he was just one of the barons of terrorism, not its face, till now.Bin Laden was based in Afghanistan, but the 9/11 Commission describes Pakistan as the country that held the key to his ability to use Afghanistan as a base for his campaign against the United States. Pakistan's military establishment was deeply preoccupied with its rivalry with India, particularly over Kashmir.That rivalry shaped Islamabad's calculations in Afghanistan.The Commission says Pakistani rulers saw the Taliban as potentially useful: they could impose order in Afghanistan and give Pakistan what its military planners called “strategic depth” against India. Pakistani intelligence officers probably knew in advance that Bin Laden was coming back to Afghanistan and may have facilitated his journey. The report also says Pakistani intelligence reportedly introduced him to Taliban leaders, partly in the hope that his camps could be made available for training Kashmiri militants.Bin Laden did not need Pakistan to be interested in his global jihad. He needed Pakistan's geopolitical calculations to create an environment in which he could operate.The United States understood this tension, but struggled to act on it.In the summer before the 1998 US embassy bombings in Kenya and Tanzania, the State Department was heavily focused on rising tensions between India and Pakistan. The Commission says this meant Washington did not aggressively challenge Pakistan over Afghanistan and Bin Laden.At the same time, American counterterrorism officials were pushing in the opposite direction.The State Department's acting counterterrorism coordinator advised Secretary of State Madeleine Albright to designate Pakistan as a state sponsor of terrorism. His argument was that, despite assurances from Pakistan's leadership, its military intelligence service continued activities supporting international terrorism, including attacks on civilian targets in Kashmir.But the South Asia bureau opposed the recommendation.Its concern was that such a move would further damage an already sensitive relationship with Pakistan, particularly after the May 1998 nuclear tests by both India and Pakistan. Albright rejected the recommendation on August 5, 1998.Two days later, al-Qaeda bombed the US embassies in Kenya and Tanzania.In 1997, an NSC policy review had already concluded that Washington needed to pay greater attention not only to India but also to Pakistan and Afghanistan. One diplomat told the Commission that the United States effectively had “no policy” towards Afghanistan at the time.But soon after that came the nuclear tests and then the Kargil war.In May 1999, Pakistani troops infiltrated the Kargil sector of Kashmir, triggering a limited war with India. The Commission records Bruce Riedel, the NSC official responsible for Pakistan, describing Islamabad as behaving like a rogue state in two areas: backing Taliban/Bin Laden terrorism and provoking war with India.The irony was that the two problems were not actually separate.Pakistan's rivalry with India helped shape its policy towards militant groups. Those militant networks operated in an ecosystem that also sheltered the Taliban. And the Taliban provided Bin Laden with the Afghan sanctuary from which al-Qaeda could develop its war against the United States.Washington was not oblivious to the threat Bin Laden posed. The CIA was actively developing plans to capture him. The Justice Department was moving towards indicting him. In April 1998, US Ambassador to the United Nations Bill Richardson travelled to Afghanistan and asked the Taliban to expel him after Bin Laden's public call for Americans to be killed.The Taliban said they did not know where he was and insisted that he was not a threat to the United States.Counterterrorism officials wanted Pakistan to exert pressure on the Taliban. President Bill Clinton discussed Bin Laden with Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif. Later, Clinton raised the issue directly with Gen Pervez Musharraf during his March 2000 visit to Pakistan and urged him to help capture Bin Laden.By then, however, the diplomatic problem had become deeply entrenched.Pakistan was simultaneously a potential partner against terrorism, a nuclear-armed rival of India, a supporter of the Taliban and a country whose military and intelligence establishment had relationships with militant groups.Washington needed Islamabad and that dependence limited how hard Washington was willing to push.Bin Laden became just one problem among several, in a region where another problem carried the possibility of nuclear war.The Commission's own summary of this period is telling: while the CIA and Justice Department pursued Bin Ladin, the State Department was concentrating more heavily on easing Indo-Pakistani nuclear tensions, ending the Afghan civil war and dealing with the Taliban's human-rights record than on driving Bin Laden out.By the time America fully understood the threat Bin Laden posed, 19 men had boarded four aircraft.
Article Summary: Washington knew Pakistan was unstable and it also knew that Islamist extremism was growing there. But the possibility of an arms race, and eventually war, between two nuclear-armed neighbours kept competing for the top spot on the American agenda. After India and Pakistan conducted nuclear tests in May 1998, that competition became even harder to ignore.

Article Title: By 2008, New Hampshire researchers had tested porous asphalt through four winters; a later study found it could cut annual salt use by 64% to 77%
Article Text:
AI Representation: Porous asphalt lets winter meltwater drain through the pavement. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 2004-to-2008 UNH parking lot study tracked porous asphalt through four winters

Faster snowmelt and less ice buildup reduced how often crews needed to plow or salt

A follow-up 2014 study quantified the salt savings across two adjacent test lots

Engineers approach pavement design in cold climates. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

The findings pointed toward a practical case for reduced-salt winter maintenance

UNH researchers conducted a study from 2004 through 2008 involving a porous asphalt parking lot in Durham that examined how well the quicker drainage and increased friction properties performed during multiple winter seasons in New England, as explained in a report from the UNH Stormwater Center detailing the results.
