In a subsequent study of the exact same site, researchers determined how much salt could be saved using the porous asphalt surface, which was about 75% per year without sacrificing safety.The first study, Water Quality and Hydrologic Performance of a Porous Asphalt Pavement as a Storm-Water Treatment Strategy in a Cold Climate, published in the Journal of Environmental Engineering in 2012, reports that the pavement's infiltration capacity ranged from about 1,490 to 2,690 cm/h even after repeated freeze-thaw cycles, despite maximum frost penetration reaching nearly 71 cm. It also found exceptional water-quality treatment performance for pollutants like petroleum hydrocarbons, zinc, and suspended solids, with no consistent seasonal decline over the four winters monitored, and with frost impacts limited by the well-drained stone reservoir beneath the surface. The system retained or infiltrated a substantial share of incoming precipitation across the monitoring period, with no seasonal drop-off in that performance, evidence that the drainage benefit persisted well beyond the warmer months.The meltwater passes through the surface rather than remaining on top, so porous asphalt surfaces accumulate fewer amounts of snow, slush and ice compared to normal dense-mix surfaces under similar treatments. In the field tests conducted, the porous surface had been observed to be comparatively cleaner and drier one hour after plowing, owing to the open-graded design of the pavement material, which removes moisture from the surface. Fewer amounts of ice formations on the surface allowed the surface to maintain its skid resistance on its own without relying on frequent applications of salts. The skid resistance measured using a British pendulum tester, yielding the British pendulum number, remained high on the porous asphalt surface even with the reduction of salt application.The second study, Assessment of Winter Maintenance of Porous Asphalt and Its Function for Chloride Source Control, published in the Journal of Transportation Engineering in 2014 (Roseen, Ballestero, Houle, Heath, and Houle), found that the porous asphalt achieved similar or better surface conditions using 64 to 77 percent less salt than the dense-mix reference surface, even though the dense-mix lot received a standard salting rate roughly four times higher, by design, as the conventional-maintenance comparison point.The earlier research mentioned this because it took a considerably lower quantity of salt to make the porous surface equally safe. The calculations made in 2014 showed that the reduction was 64-77%, which is an average of 75% less salt used per year, while the friction on the surface of porous asphalt was equal to or even higher than on the conventional one. There were instances when the porous surface, despite not being salted at all, had better performance results than the conventional one, even if it was fully salted.The roughly 75 percent reduction in salt use is valuable for more than just maintenance budgets: road salt is a well-documented source of chloride pollution in groundwater and surface waters, so less salt applied means less chloride released into those waters in the first place. The findings of the tests of the porous asphalt mentioned above suggest that it is the pavement design itself, not the change in salting technology or equipment, that leads to such results.Taken together, the two UNH studies suggest sustained drainage performance over time and show a substantial, if lot-specific, reduction in salt use with this pavement. However, there are some caveats involved. The data for the salt reductions have been lot-specific, depending upon the amount of shade in each lot and the condition in which the stone reservoir underneath has been maintained over time, because clogging caused by sediments and organic matter will cause reductions in the infiltration capacity of the pavement. Nonetheless, the New Hampshire studies still represent one of the most comprehensive long-term datasets concerning the winter performance of porous asphalt.
Article Summary: Porous asphalt lets winter meltwater drain through the pavement. A 2004-to-2008 UNH parking lot study tracked porous asphalt through four winters. Faster snowmelt and less ice buildup reduced how often crews needed to plow or salt.

Article Title: In 2019, Los Angeles County coated streets across a 0.64-square-kilometer neighborhood; surfaces were up to 9°F cooler, but ten months later the cooling effect had fallen by about 1.8°F
Article Text:
AI Representation: A reflective road coating helped cool Los Angeles streets, though its cooling benefit diminished over the following months. Image credits: Chatgpt

A 2022 paper analyzed the 2019 Covina deployment's albedo shift

, "Measuring the impacts of a real-world neighborhood-scale cool pavement deployment on albedo and temperatures in Los Angeles,"

Ten months later, albedo had fallen back to between 0.16 and 0.24

A 2022 Pacoima project treated over 700,000 square feet of asphalt

September 2022 heatwave measurements showed up to 3.4°F of air cooling

Together, the two studies point to a shared maintenance problem

Asphalt underlines the albedo/temperature contrast discussed in the Winnetka results. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

Los Angeles County's Department of Public Works, in 2019, applied a solar-reflective coating on roads in an area covering 0.64 km² of Covina, California, in order to determine whether a cooling effect could be achieved using a simple paving technology. As Ko and colleagues later reported in Environmental Research Letters, the surface temperature fell by as much as 9°F (5°C), but after ten months of weathering and vehicle traffic, that cooling effect had weakened by 1.8°F. A more recent, larger experiment in the Pacoima neighborhood has also provided useful data on the method’s practicality.Analysis of the impact of the Covina project is provided in the studypublished in the peer-reviewed journal Environmental Research Letters in 2022. According to the authors, average pavement albedo increased by 0.18, from 0.08 to 0.26, resulting in a maximum neighborhood‑averaged temperature reduction of 5 °C at the surface and 0.2 °C in the near‑surface air. The authors also report that cooling efficiency declined by about 1 °C as albedo fell by roughly 30%. According to the authors, this is among the first field studies to measure air-temperature reductions from cool pavements, and they note that further work is needed to assess trade-offs for pedestrian comfort. To quantify the impact of cool pavements on surface and air temperatures, the researchers took both mobile and stationary measurements, comparing coated streets with nearby uncoated streets to distinguish the coating’s cooling effect from broader seasonal temperature changes.However, the effect faded quickly. About ten months after installation, researchers found that the coating’s albedo had fallen to between 0.16 and 0.24, depending on the location, from 0.26 immediately after application. That change in albedo reduced the road-surface cooling effect by about 1°C, or 1.8°F, compared with the initial result. For city officials, the result matters because it shifts cool pavement from a one-time installation to an ongoing maintenance task. If the effect decreases by one-fifth during only ten months, then the pavement needs re-coating quite regularly if the city wishes to retain the initial cooling effect.A year-long observational study, Micrometeorological effects and thermal-environmental benefits of cool pavements: findings from a detailed observational field study in Pacoima, California, published in Environmental Research Communications , tracked results across an entire year using a mix of ground sensors, drone imagery, and satellite data. The study found that the reflective surface reduced surface and air temperatures in the urban canopy layer by less than 2°C, though it at times raised the mean radiant temperature by up to 1.2°C, with no evidence of glare or photochemical damage. Using a broader suite of instruments, the researchers were able to examine not only temperature impacts but also secondary effects of reflective surfaces, such as glare, air‑quality changes associated with UV reflectance, and pedestrian thermal comfort.As the Pacoima study reported, coated surfaces had air temperatures 1.9°C, or 3.4°F, cooler than those on control surfaces during the afternoons of the September 2022 heatwave. On other summer days that were not within the heatwave period, the highest variation in surface temperature between the coated surfaces and the control surfaces was 12.2°C, which was higher than the variations observed in the previous cool pavement research. Just like the case in Covina stated above, the degree of the cooling effect was very variable depending on location and weather.Both of these research projects, however, end up with one and the same idea through different perspectives. The studies suggest that reflective coatings can reduce surface and air temperatures, but effectiveness varies with coating age, type and weather conditions. In this respect, the Covina study is particularly valuable for tracking how quickly the reflective effect degrades over time, while the Pacoima study, which also spans roughly a year, is especially useful for showing how the cooling effect varies with weather conditions, including during a summer heatwave.Neither project, however, settles how effective cool pavements are at reducing pedestrian-level air temperatures. According to the scientists involved in the Pacoima project, reflective pavements can help with heat mitigation but are not a substitute for the shade trees provide. The larger takeaway from both studies is that the cooling effect of cool pavements is not permanent, a factor cities need to weigh when planning maintenance schedules, reapplication frequency, and how long a given installation stays effective.
Article Summary: Los Angeles County's Department of Public Works applied a solar-reflective coating on roads in an area covering 0.64 km² of Covina, California, in 2019. Researchers found that the coating’s albedo had fallen to between 0.16 and 0.24, depending on the location, from 0.26 immediately after application. After ten months of weathering and vehicle traffic, that cooling effect had weakened by 1.8°F.

Article Title: In 1914, Tom Yawkey’s uncle bought Cat Island and nearby coastal land in Georgetown County; decades later, the 24,000-acre preserve sheltered woodpeckers and wetland birds
Article Text:
Representative image of a protected coastal marsh and forest preserve providing habitat for woodpeckers and wetland birds. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

From private hunting land to a conservation legacy

A refuge for birds, wetlands and threatened wildlife

American Alliagator. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Why a century-old decision still matters

In 1914, businessman William Yawkey’s uncle bought coastal land in South Carolina, setting in motion a conservation story that would unfold over more than a century. What began as a small holding along the shoreline of Georgetown County eventually became the Tom Yawkey Wildlife Centre, a 24,000-acre protected landscape where marshes, wetlands, pine forests, beaches and maritime forests now provide habitat for a remarkable range of wildlife.According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources , Tom Yawkey inherited the coastal property in 1925, after his uncle had purchased land there in 1914, and began investing in its conservation and preservation. In 1926, he purchased the remaining tracts of land from the South Island Hunting Club and began improving the property with wildlife protection in mind. The property eventually became the 24,000-acre Tom Yawkey Wildlife Center, which includes North Island, South Island, Sand Island and most of Cat Island at the mouth of Winyah Bay. Covering about 31 square miles, the preserve contains marshes, managed wetlands, upland pine forests, beaches and maritime forests, and is managed as a wildlife preserve, research area and waterfowl refuge.Tom Yawkey is better known to many Americans as the longtime owner of the Boston Red Sox. But away from baseball, he developed a deep interest in wildlife and land management. According to the Tom Yawkey Wildlife Center , Yawkey was a self-taught ornithologist who spent years studying land-management techniques before bringing professional wildlife biologists into the effort.His aim was not simply to leave the property untouched, but to manage its varied habitats for waterfowl and other wildlife. The preserve includes freshwater and brackish wetlands, pine forests, maritime habitats, beaches and rice fields, creating a mix of ecosystems that support coastal wildlife. Currently, the research program at the centre includes studies of birds, alligators, sea turtles, flora, wetlands, and other parts of the coastal environment, which has encouraged more than 150 scientific papers to be published by the staff of this centre.According to a study published in The Anatomical Record , researchers examined a wild adult alligator that had been captured and measured five times over seven years at the Yawkey Wildlife Centre. The animal showed no discernible growth during that period, suggesting it had already reached skeletal maturity. Examination of its limb bones provided further evidence that growth had ceased. The study built on a much longer record of alligator research at the centre. Mark-recapture work there has been under way since 1979, allowing scientists to follow individual animals over periods of several decades. That long-term record makes the Yawkey property especially valuable for studying how animals live, grow and reproduce over time.The birds are among the creatures that benefit from this protected landscape. The landscape features several habitats which provide the birds with opportunities for both food and nesting. In 2022, according to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources (SCDNR), the Yawkey Foundation donated another 269 acres on Cat Island to the department. The addition included 161 acres of upland pine forest habitat for the federally endangered red-cockaded woodpecker and 108 acres of managed wetland habitat for waterfowl, wading birds and shorebirds. The donation also helped preserve an important historic landmark, the Belle Isle Rice Mill Chimney, which is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Standing 34 feet high, the chimney and its surrounding landscape offer a reminder of the rice culture that once shaped the South Carolina Lowcountry.This blend of natural and cultural history defines the centre. The islands it protects are far from untouched wilderness; they bear evidence of Indigenous and Gullah Geechee communities, historic agriculture, coastal habitation and changing patterns of land use. Archaeological and shoreline studies are currently being conducted to document and protect culturally significant sites threatened by sea-level rise and erosion. The centre also provides habitat for loggerhead sea turtles, while its wetlands support alligators and a wide range of other coastal wildlife. Alligator nesting research, for instance, continues at the site, highlighting the centre’s role in both conservation and scientific study.In 2026, the Tom Yawkey Wildlife Center traces its conservation history back a century to 1926, when Tom Yawkey expanded the coastal property he had inherited and began acquiring additional land with wildlife protection in mind. The property remained under his stewardship for decades before he left it to the State of South Carolina in 1976. It was dedicated as a Heritage Preserve the following year, establishing the foundation for its continued protection as a public conservation area. Today, the 24,000-acre centre protects more than 7,000 acres of longleaf pine habitat that supports the federally endangered red-cockaded woodpecker, as well as wetlands important to waterfowl and other birds and beaches used by nesting loggerhead sea turtles. The landscape has therefore retained the conservation purpose that Yawkey began developing in the 1920s, while becoming part of South Carolina's long-term effort to protect its coastal wildlife.
Article Summary: The Tom Yawkey Wildlife Centre is a 24,000-acre protected landscape in South Carolina. It includes North Island, South Island, Sand Island and most of Cat Island at the mouth of Winyah Bay. The preserve contains marshes, managed wetlands, upland pine forests, beaches and maritime forests, and is managed as a wildlife preserve, research area and waterfowl refuge.

Article Title: After Trump renamed Lake Ontario 'Lake America,' a Pennsylvania Republican now wants Lake Erie renamed 'Lake Pennsylvania'
Article Text:
David Maloney, Trump

Why Maloney wants Lake Erie renamed

Where the name Lake Erie comes from

Would 'Lake Pennsylvania' become official?

President Donald Trump ’s decision to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” has now been followed by a similar proposal involving another Great Lake. A Republican lawmaker in Pennsylvania is preparing a resolution seeking to rename Lake Erie as “Lake Pennsylvania”.State Representative David Maloney argues that the state has a strong economic and cultural connection with the Great Lake. He is expected to urge President Donald Trump, Congress and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum to take steps towards changing the lake’s name, according to a an official statement issued by him, Newsweek reported.Maloney represents Pennsylvania’s 130th Legislative District in Berks County. He said Pennsylvanians regularly travel to Lake Erie for boating, fishing and family visits, with visitors spending money along the state’s shoreline. He also referred to research by Pennsylvania Sea Grant and said Pennsylvania stocked almost 500,000 yearling steelhead in 2025, which he said was about 40% of the steelhead stocked across the lake.The proposal comes about two weeks after Trump signed an executive order directing US federal agencies to use the name “Lake America” for Lake Ontario.Trump signed the order on August 27, during growing tensions between the United States and Canada over trade. The order requires US federal agencies to use the new name on maps, documents and databases.The Lake Ontario decision itself has faced resistance in Canada and parts of the United States. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the name change, saying the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. Several US governors in the Great Lakes region also dismissed the move.Maloney said Pennsylvania has a particular connection with Lake Erie, which borders the state. He pointed to recreation and fishing as reasons for the proposed name change.“Ohio has plenty of shoreline. New York already has two Great Lakes. Canada has four others,” Maloney said.His office told Newsweek that the proposal is based on how Pennsylvanians care for the lake and how residents of other states also visit it for recreation and fishing. “Be proud and own it,” the office said.Lake Erie is shared by the United States and Canada. Ontario lies along its northern shore, while Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania and New York border it on the American side. It is the smallest Great Lake by volume and the shallowest.According to the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, the name comes from the Indigenous people who lived along its southern shore when Europeans reached the area in the early 1600s.“Erie” is a shortened form of the Iroquoian word “Erielhonan”, which means “long tail” and refers to the eastern cougar,The National Museum of the Great Lakes says Europeans discovered Lake Erie last among the Great Lakes. Control of the lake was also strategically important because it provided access to areas above Niagara Falls.Maloney’s proposal would face the same broader issue surrounding any US attempt to change the name of a body of water shared with another country.The US Board on Geographic Names says proposals to change existing geographic names require a compelling reason and evidence of support. The board generally discourages changes to existing names.If the federal government approved the change, “Lake Pennsylvania” would become the name used by US federal departments and agencies. But Canada has its own geographical naming authorities, so a US decision would not automatically change the lake’s official name in Canada.
Article Summary: State Representative David Maloney argues that the state has a strong economic and cultural connection with the Great Lake. He is expected to urge President Donald Trump, Congress and Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum to take steps towards changing the lake’s name.

Article Title: Saudi crown prince allegedly asked Trump to hit Houthis; US president declined: Report
Article Text: US President Donald Trump rejected phone calls from Saudi Arabia's crown prince Mohammed Bin Salman twice, urging him to launch strikes against Houthis, Axios reported, citing US officials.According to the report, US officials said Trump declined the request because the US has no plans to intervene directly for now."On Thursday, as Houthi forces advanced on the coastal city of Mokha and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces retreated, MBS called Trump to brief him on the deteriorating situation," US officials told Axios."Several hours later, MBS called again and urged Trump to order US strikes against the Houthis. Trump declined, but the administration will provide Saudi Arabia with intelligence on the Houthis and targeting data," they added.According to a senior Trump administration official, Washington's priority is keeping the Red Sea open while leaving the broader fight to its regional partners."The United States is focused on protecting our core national security interests — such as ensuring freedom of navigation in the Red Sea — while empowering our regional partners to take the lead in managing and resolving regional security challenges," the official told Axios."We are in continuous dialogue with Saudi Arabia and the republic of Yemen government regarding regional stability," the official added.This comes after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi militants seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha and advanced towards the Hanish islands, bringing them closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and raising the prospect of a major new threat to one of the world's most vital shipping routes.Mokha is about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a waterway that connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden and through which about 12% of the world's goods are typically shipped.Houthi forces have pushed Saudi-backed government troops south towards Dhubab, directly opposite Perim island at the entrance to the strait, according to two Yemeni government sources. Control of the area could put the Houthis in a position to threaten maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb.The Houthis kept mostly to the sidelines when the Iran war began, but over the summer, the rebels increased attacks against Yemen's internationally recognized government and declared a blockade on Saudi Arabia, which supports it.While the Houthis have their own reasons for fighting the Saudis, the conflict also serves Iran's interests by ramping up pressure on the American-allied oil producer as Tehran seeks leverage against the US.
Article Summary: Houthi militants seized the key Red Sea port of Mokha and advanced towards the Hanish islands. Control of the area could put the Houthis in a position to threaten maritime traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. The conflict also serves Iran's interests by ramping up pressure on the American-allied oil producer.

Article Title: After 9/11, Canada’s tiny town of Gander sheltered 7,000 Americans for days, providing food and refuge as 38 planes landed there following the attack
Article Text:
A Canadian town suddenly filled with stranded American passengers

Residents opened their homes and community buildings

The response became a symbol of Canadian generosity

The story later reached Broadway

Gander still remembers what happened

The relationship with America has since changed

Canadians still distinguish Americans from their government

A new generation sees America differently

The welcome has not disappeared

Long before the trade tariffs, barriers and diplomatic tensions between the US and Canada, there was a time when thousands of Americans found unexpected refuge in a tiny Canadian town after 9/11. On September 11, 2001, residents of a small Canadian town thousands of miles from New York suddenly found themselves caring for thousands of strangers caught up in an unprecedented crisis. When the United States closed its airspace following the terrorist attacks, 38 passenger planes crossing the Atlantic were diverted to Gander in Newfoundland and Labrador. The town, with a population of fewer than 10,000 people, suddenly had to accommodate around 7,000 passengers and crew. Schools, churches, community centres and homes became temporary shelters, while residents supplied food, clothing and other essentials. What began as an emergency quickly became an extraordinary display of hospitality, with ordinary people opening their doors to frightened travellers who had no idea when they would be able to continue their journeys.Gander was uniquely positioned to receive the diverted aircraft because of its long aviation history.Located on the northeastern island of Newfoundland, the town had once been a major refuelling point for aircraft crossing the North Atlantic. Its airport was among the world's most important aviation hubs before advances in aircraft technology made longer non-stop flights possible. On September 11, however, its historic role suddenly returned in dramatic fashion. As flights were diverted from US airspace, 38 aircraft landed at Gander International Airport, bringing thousands of passengers into a community that had never expected to accommodate so many people at once.The scale of the challenge was enormous. Gander and nearby communities had to find places for thousands of passengers while aircraft remained grounded and travellers waited for information. Residents responded by transforming everyday spaces into temporary shelters. Schools, churches and public buildings were opened, while people brought food, clothing, toiletries and other necessities. Some locals invited complete strangers into their homes. The response was not limited to organised emergency services. Shopkeepers, teachers, cooks, hotel workers, students and ordinary families all found ways to help people who had suddenly been separated from their normal journeys and, in many cases, from their families.The stranded passengers could not simply leave the airport and continue their journeys. They remained in the region for several days as the international aviation system dealt with the unprecedented disruption. During that period, the people of Gander and surrounding communities continued providing meals, accommodation and practical assistance. Passengers were able to contact relatives, receive medical help when needed and find basic comforts while waiting. The Canadian government's account of the episode records more than 6,500 passengers and crew being accommodated in Gander, while the widely told story of the town often rounds the figure to around 7,000 people.What happened in Gander gradually became one of the most enduring stories of kindness to emerge from the aftermath of 9/11. There were no elaborate preparations for such an influx of people and no expectation that the town would suddenly become a refuge for thousands of international travellers. Yet residents responded with an instinctive willingness to help. Their actions became a powerful example of how a small community could respond to a crisis on an international scale. The episode also strengthened the already close relationship between Canada and the United States at a moment when Americans were experiencing shock, fear and uncertainty.The extraordinary events in Gander eventually became the subject of the musical Come From Away. The production tells the story of passengers stranded in Newfoundland and the residents who cared for them. It brought the experience of Gander to audiences far beyond Canada and the United States and became an internationally recognised stage production. The musical's popularity helped turn what might otherwise have remained a remarkable local episode into a lasting part of the public memory of 9/11.More than two decades later, the events remain deeply embedded in the town's identity. Gander continues to commemorate September 11, with the anniversary serving as a reminder of the unusual connection formed between the community and the passengers who arrived there unexpectedly. The North Atlantic Aviation Museum and other local attractions also preserve the town's aviation history and its connection to the events of 2001. For many residents, however, the most important legacy is not the fame that followed but the simple principle that shaped their response at the time. People needed help, and the community helped them.The warmth associated with Gander's response to 9/11 stands in sharp contrast to the strained relationship between Canada and the United States today. Under President Donald Trump, disputes over tariffs and trade have created significant tension between the two neighbouring countries. Canadian frustration has grown as Washington has pursued policies that Ottawa considers damaging to Canadian economic interests. The deterioration has been particularly striking because Canada and the United States have historically maintained one of the world's closest economic and political relationships.Despite the political tensions, the Gander story shows that hostility towards US policies does not necessarily translate into hostility towards ordinary Americans. People in the town interviewed for the recent account continued to express a willingness to help Americans in another emergency. Some even made a clear distinction between the American people and the administration in Washington. That distinction is particularly striking because some Americans visiting Canada today reportedly feel the need to apologise for their government's actions, creating an almost complete reversal of the emotional dynamic seen after 9/11.The shift may be particularly significant among younger Canadians who have grown up with a very different image of the United States. Older Canadians often remember decades of close cultural, economic and personal connections with their southern neighbour, including frequent travel across the border and a strong influence from American television and popular culture. Younger Canadians have increasingly encountered the United States through a period of political polarisation and disputes over issues ranging from trade to reproductive rights. For them, the America remembered fondly by older generations may be more distant and less familiar.Yet the remarkable thing about Gander is that its basic attitude towards people in need appears unchanged. The town that opened its doors to thousands of frightened passengers in 2001 remains willing to welcome visitors from the United States, provided the relationship is based on mutual respect. That gives the Gander story a meaning that goes beyond the events of one terrible day. Twenty-five years after 9/11, the town remains a reminder that international relationships are not built only by governments. Sometimes they are shaped by ordinary people who decide to help a stranger when there is no obligation to do so.
Article Summary: 38 passenger planes were diverted to Gander in Newfoundland and Labrador. The town, with a population of fewer than 10,000 people, suddenly had to accommodate around 7,000 passengers and crew. Schools, churches, community centres and homes became temporary shelters, while residents supplied food, clothing and other essentials. The response became a symbol of Canadian generosity.

Article Title: In 1976, a Vermont town buried a time capsule that included a joint, a garter belt and birth-control packaging; 50 years later, it opened it and plans a new one for 2076
Article Text:
Representative image

A message from the bicentennial year

The unexpected contents

What happens when the future arrives

A town gathering becomes a history lesson

Preparing a new capsule for 2076

What Warren might say about 2026

A conversation across generations

In 1976, as the United States celebrated its bicentennial, residents of Warren, Vermont, decided to leave a message for the future. They filled a time capsule with objects that reflected everyday life, local humour and the era’s changing culture, then buried it beneath the town. Among the contents were a joint, a garter belt and birth-control packaging, items that offered a candid glimpse of what people considered worth remembering at the time. Fifty years later, Warren opened the capsule, turning an ordinary town gathering into an unexpected lesson in social history. As reported by The Valley Reporter, the community is now preparing to bury a new capsule for 2076, giving future residents their own chance to discover how Warren lived, laughed and thought in 2026.The original capsule was created during a year of national celebration. In 1976, communities across the country marked the 200th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence with parades, concerts, historical displays and local projects. Warren joined that movement by creating a physical record of its own moment in time.Time capsules often combine official history with ordinary objects.A newspaper may sit beside a school photograph, a local business card or a handwritten note from a child. The intention is usually to preserve a snapshot, but the most revealing items are often those that people might otherwise overlook. Everyday packaging, clothing and personal objects reveal how people lived more honestly than formal speeches or ceremonial documents.Warren’s capsule appears to have embraced that spirit. It was not simply a polished collection designed to present the town in the best possible light. The inclusion of a joint, a garter belt and birth-control packaging reflected the humour, openness and social changes of the 1970s. These objects may have surprised people when the capsule was opened, but they also made the collection feel recognisably human.The joint offered a direct connection to the counterculture of the period, when attitudes toward marijuana were changing and young people challenged many traditional social norms. Its presence in the capsule suggested that Warren’s residents were willing to acknowledge parts of everyday life that would not normally appear in an official historical archive.The garter belt added another layer of personal and cultural history. Clothing often carries information about social expectations, fashion and intimacy. An item that may have seemed cheeky or comic in 1976 can become a useful historical clue decades later, showing how people understood gender, relationships and private life.The birth-control packaging reflected the changing landscape of reproductive health and personal choice. By the 1970s, contraception had become an important part of public discussion, particularly after major legal and social changes earlier in the decade. Including the packaging turned a private consumer object into a record of the era’s wider conversations about relationships, family planning and independence.Together, the items created a portrait that was more complicated than a standard civic display. They showed a town willing to preserve not only its official milestones but also the humour and awkwardness of ordinary life.When people bury a time capsule, they often imagine that the future will be dramatically different from the present. They picture new technology, changed fashions and unfamiliar customs. What they cannot know is which details will seem important to the people who eventually open it.For Warren residents in 2026, the capsule’s contents made the past feel both distant and surprisingly familiar. The objects were undeniably tied to the 1970s, yet the impulse behind them remains recognisable. People still use humour to mark community events, still worry about how they will be remembered and still choose ordinary objects to explain their lives to strangers in the future.The opening also raised questions about what the original creators hoped to communicate. Did they expect future residents to laugh, be shocked or study the contents seriously? Perhaps they understood that a time capsule works best when it contains a mixture of all three. Historical value does not require an object to be solemn. Sometimes the most revealing evidence comes wrapped in embarrassment or amusement.The capsule opening was more than an archaeological exercise. It gave residents an opportunity to gather across generations and discuss how Warren had changed since 1976. Older residents could explain the context behind the objects, while younger people could compare the capsule’s contents with their own experiences.Events like this help local history feel personal. National anniversaries and major political events matter, but community identity is also built from small memories. A local time capsule can preserve the names of residents, the jokes they shared, the products they used and the things they believed their descendants might find interesting.The unusual items also made the history accessible. Children and teenagers may not be drawn immediately to a typed civic report, but a mysterious box containing a joint, a garter belt and old packaging invites questions. Who put these objects inside? Why were they funny or meaningful? What would people in 2076 find strange about the way we live now?After opening the old capsule, Warren plans to create and bury a new one for the town’s future residents. The project offers an opportunity to reflect on what deserves preservation in 2026. Technology will almost certainly play a role, with residents considering whether to include photographs, digital files, local newspapers, school projects, menus, product packaging and personal letters.Yet the organisers face a challenge that earlier generations did not encounter at the same scale. Digital information can be easy to create but difficult to preserve. Files may become unreadable as software and storage systems change. A physical object, by contrast, can be understood even when the technology of its era has disappeared. The new capsule may therefore need a mixture of printed material and carefully selected objects that remain accessible without specialised equipment.The selection process is likely to generate its own debate. Should the capsule include a smartphone, a face mask, a grocery receipt, a school assignment or a note about local housing costs? Which parts of 2026 will seem essential in 2076, and which will appear trivial? The uncertainty is part of the appeal.A capsule created in 2026 could reflect a period marked by rapid technological change, climate concerns, political division and shifting ideas about community. It might include evidence of how people communicated, worked, travelled and entertained themselves. It could document local responses to extreme weather, changes in farming or debates about development.Personal contributions may be just as valuable as official records. A child’s drawing, a family photograph or a handwritten prediction could reveal more about the emotional atmosphere of the town than a formal statement. Future residents may be fascinated by things that seem ordinary today, such as how people paid for goods, watched films, stored photographs or navigated without relying entirely on digital services.The original capsule shows that there is no need to make the new collection overly polished. If Warren wants the 2076 opening to feel authentic, the capsule should include humour, imperfections and objects that capture the full range of local life.Time capsules are often described as messages to the future, but they also create conversations in the present. Preparing a new capsule encourages residents to ask what their town values and how they want to be remembered. Opening the old one encourages them to think about the people who lived there before them, not as distant historical figures but as neighbours with similar hopes, jokes and uncertainties.The 1976 capsule’s unusual contents made that connection especially strong. The people who selected those items could not have predicted how the world would look 50 years later, but they understood that future residents would be curious about the private and playful sides of their lives.Now Warren is returning the gesture. The new capsule will wait beneath the town for another half century, when a different generation will open it and decide what it says about 2026. It may contain objects that seem ordinary today but become fascinating clues later. It may also contain something as unexpected as the original joint, garter belt or birth-control packaging.
Article Summary: Residents of Warren, Vermont, filled a time capsule with objects that reflected everyday life, local humour and the era’s changing culture. Among the contents were a joint, a garter belt and birth-control packaging. Fifty years later, Warren opened the capsule, turning an ordinary town gathering into an unexpected lesson in social history.

Article Title: Pakistan blinks on Houthis, walks back Saudi defence warning within 24 hours
Article Text:
Pakistan has clarified that there are no current discussions about military responses related to the Mecca defense pact, following recent warnings from its defense minister.

No plans to expand Mecca pact

Pakistan appears to have taken a step back from its strong warning to the Houthis a day earlier, with Islamabad on Thursday saying that no military response under the newly signed Mecca defence pact is currently being discussed. The comments came despite its defence minister warning that the agreement could become operational if the Yemen conflict spilled into Saudi Arabia.“There is no such thing under discussion right now ... When time comes (we) will act under the agreement,” Pakistan foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said on Thursday, referring to the pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye last month.The apparent shift comes a day after defence minister Khawaja Asif warned that the pact could become operational if the Yemen conflict spilled into Saudi Arabia. He said Pakistan was “bound by the terms and conditions of this pact” and would honour its commitments if required.Asif had also warned the Houthis that if they tried to extend the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia, “the clauses of this pact over confronting aggression will become operative”. At the same time, he stressed that the agreement was defensive and did not authorise the three countries to independently launch offensive operations against another country.The latest clarification comes as Houthi attacks on Saudi cities and energy infrastructure have intensified.The Mecca joint defence agreement was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7 in Mecca to strengthen collective deterrence and defence cooperation. Under the agreement, “any armed attack against any one of the three States shall be regarded as an attack against them all.” The pact also calls for enhanced defence cooperation among the three countries.Pakistan also ruled out any immediate expansion of the Mecca defence alliance, with foreign ministry spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan saying “there are no plans to expand the Mecca alliance.”The clarification comes after earlier discussions about potentially bringing other countries into the arrangement. Pakistan's foreign ministry had previously said that any country seeking to join would be considered in consultation with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, but that there were no formal applications or new names at that stage.
Article Summary: Pakistan says there are no current discussions about military responses to the Mecca defense pact. Defence minister Khawaja Asif had warned that the pact could become operational if the Yemen conflict spilled into Saudi Arabia. The Mecca joint defence agreement was signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye on August 7.

Article Title: Osama bin Laden had Taliban rival assassinated 2 days before 9/11 attack
Article Text:
Osama bin Laden (File photo)

Ahmad Shah Massoud, the prominent Afghan resistance leader and one of the Taliban's strongest rivals, was assassinated on September 9, 2001, just two days before the 9/11 attacks, in a killing believed to have been ordered by al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden as a favour to his Taliban hosts, according to a Newsweek report.Massoud, who led Afghanistan's Northern Alliance, was killed while being interviewed at his camp in the Panjshir Valley by two men posing as Belgian television journalists. The two al-Qaeda operatives had concealed explosives inside a video camera despite undergoing security checks before meeting the resistance leader, Newsweek reported.The Northern Alliance did not officially confirm Massoud's death until September 15.Massoud had built a powerful insurgent network in northern Afghanistan and remained a major obstacle to Taliban control of the country. His influence and popularity also made him a key figure among forces opposed to the Taliban.According to Newsweek, bin Laden was believed to have ordered Massoud's assassination partly as a favour to his Taliban hosts and partly because he expected the United States to launch retaliatory strikes following the planned September 11 attacks Eliminating Massoud was also strategically important because bin Laden understood the Afghan leader's value as a military commander and political figure who could have played a significant role in any campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.The assassination alarmed the CIA, which had maintained contacts with Massoud and other Afghan opposition figures.Gary Berntsen, the CIA officer who later led the agency's first team into Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks, recalled that the news "made me feel sick to my stomach ... I figured this was the end of the Northern Alliance."CIA director George Tenet was less pessimistic, noting that the agency had maintained relationships with other Afghan warlords.Tenet later wrote, "Masood's [sic] brutal murder by al-Qaeda on the eve of the 9/11 attacks might have undone our plan before it got under way if we hadn't maintained contact with other warlords in the north."Tenet's meeting with Pakistan's ISI chiefOn the day Massoud was assassinated, Tenet was having lunch with Pakistani Gen. Mahmood Ahmed, then head of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI), Pakistan's main intelligence agency.According to Tenet's account, he pressed Mahmood on al-Qaeda and Taliban leader Mullah Omar. Mahmood assured him that Omar wanted what was best for the Afghan people and suggested that the CIA try bribing key Taliban officials to secure bin Laden's surrender."As gracious as he could be over the lunch table, the guy was immovable when it came to the Taliban and al-Qaeda," Tenet later wrote.Mahmood would be in Washington on September 11, when he met senior US lawmakers including Senate Intelligence Committee chairman Bob Graham, House Intelligence Committee chairman Porter Goss and Senator Jon Kyl.In the aftermath of the attacks, Mahmood held further meetings with US officials as Washington pressed Pakistan to cooperate in its campaign against terrorism. US military forces were also clandestinely deployed to Pakistani territory as the Bush administration prepared its response to the attacks.Massoud's assassination therefore came at a critical moment. Two days before the attacks that transformed US foreign policy and triggered the war in Afghanistan, one of the Taliban's most formidable opponents had already been eliminated.
Article Summary: Ahmad Shah Massoud was assassinated on September 9, 2001, two days before the 9/11 attacks. Massoud led Afghanistan's Northern Alliance and was a major obstacle to Taliban control. Al-Qaeda chief Osama bin Laden believed to have ordered Massoud's assassination.

Article Title: BLA claims 52 Pakistani personnel killed in 28 operations across Balochistan
Article Text:
BLA claims major offensive across Balochistan, 52 Pakistani personnel killed in 28 operations

The Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has claimed that it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7, killing 52 Pakistani military personnel and injuring several others.The claims come against the backdrop of separate military operations in the province, with the Pakistani Army saying security forces killed 11 militants in Kharan and Washuk districts on September 6 and 7.According to the Balochistan Post, in a weekly statement, BLA spokesperson Jeeyand Baloch said the group conducted operations in Pasni, Kharan, Kalat, Turbat, Mastung, Surab, Tump, Pishin, Jhal Magsi, Noshki, Chagai and Quetta. The group also said 12 of its rebels were killed during clashes with Pakistani forces.The BLA’s account, as reported by TBP, began with an operation on September 1 at Zero Point in Pasni, Gwadar. The group claimed that it attacked a joint police and Levies post and checkpoints operated by Customs and the Coastal Police, seized weapons and military equipment, and later destroyed the positions.It said an ambush on a convoy at Albat in Kharan and an attack at Garari in Kalat targeted personnel transporting armoured vehicles, with three vehicles severely damaged and personnel killed or injured.On September 2, the group claimed an IED attack followed by an ambush at Guro in Mastung’s Khadkocha area, alleging four personnel were killed and more than seven injured. A day later, it claimed an STOS attack at Hajika in Surab, killing seven personnel and destroying one vehicle.The BLA claimed its Fateh Squad killed 18 Pakistani military personnel and injured five in Pishin’s Ziarat Cross. It also claimed attacks in Tump, Mastung, Kalat and Jhal Magsi, and took responsibility for the killings of Abdul Rehman Langove and Rehmat Saeed in Quetta, alleging both worked for Pakistani forces.Separately, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), the Pakistani Army’s media wing, said eight militants were killed in Kharan on September 6 after security forces intercepted a group allegedly attempting to block a road. Another three were killed in Washuk the following day, it said.The BLA’s casualty and operational claims have not been independently verified.Meanwhile, TBP reported two fresh alleged enforced disappearances in Balochistan, while five previously missing people had returned home. It said Ali Baloch was allegedly detained by Pakistani forces in Mastung on August 23 and remains unaccounted for.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) claims it carried out 28 operations across Balochistan between September 1 and 7. BLA claims 52 Pakistani military personnel killed in 28 operations. Pakistani Army says security forces killed 11 militants in Kharan and Washuk districts.

Article Title: Pakistan orders medical institutions to expel Afghan students, halt fresh admissions amid Kabul tensions
Article Text:
Afghan students face expulsion from Pakistan medical colleges amid rising tensions

Poll Vote & Share your view Should Afghan students already enrolled be allowed to continue their studies in Pakistan? Yes, they should be allowed No, they should return to Afghanistan 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Pakistan has ordered medical and dental institutions across the country to stop admitting Afghan students and remove those already enrolled, amid worsening relations between Islamabad and Kabul, a senior government official said on Wednesday.The decision could affect hundreds of Afghan students pursuing undergraduate medical and dental courses in Pakistan, including students close to completing their degrees.Under a directive issued to medical and dental institutions, the Pakistan Medical and Dental Council has barred colleges from admitting or placing Afghan students during the current academic session, a senior health ministry official said.Afghan students already enrolled in medical and dental programmes have also been instructed to return to Afghanistan, the official said.The measure applies specifically to Afghan nationals and does not affect students from other countries, the official added. He said the decision was taken against the backdrop of deteriorating relations between the two neighbouring countries.However, Pakistan's Foreign Office said Afghan students who hold valid travel and residency documents can continue to apply for visa extensions under existing rules.Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan told Dawn that under Pakistan's Illegal Foreigners Repatriation Plan, foreign nationals without valid passports and visas are staying in the country illegally and can be deported.“However, Pakistani authorities are continuing to process visa extension applications from Afghan students in accordance with our existing policy, rules and regulations,” he said.King Edward Medical University (KEMU) in Lahore has become the first public-sector institution to implement the directive, according to a university official.“Twenty-two Afghan students are currently studying at KEMU, and they have been given 24 hours to complete the necessary legal and administrative formalities,” the official told PTI.The order comes as tensions between Islamabad and Kabul remain high, particularly over Pakistan's allegations that the banned Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan operates from sanctuaries in Afghanistan. The Taliban administration has denied the allegation.Relations deteriorated further following a series of explosions in Kabul on October 9 last year and subsequent cross-border exchanges that resulted in casualties and damage on both sides.The latest order comes against the backdrop of Pakistan's broader campaign to deport Afghan nationals without valid documentation.Millions of Afghans have sought refuge in Pakistan over several decades after fleeing successive conflicts. Hundreds of thousands more entered the country after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021.Pakistan launched a large-scale deportation drive against undocumented foreigners in 2023 and renewed the campaign in April last year after cancelling hundreds of thousands of residence permits held by Afghan nationals.In June, Pakistan's interior ministry directed authorities to arrest Afghan nationals found living in the country without valid visas from July 10.More than one million Afghan nationals were deported from Pakistan last year alone.
Article Summary: Pakistan has ordered medical and dental institutions across the country to stop admitting Afghan students and remove those already enrolled. The decision comes amid worsening relations between Islamabad and Kabul. Pakistan's Foreign Office said Afghan students who hold valid travel and residency documents can continue to apply for visa extensions.

Article Title: 'Attack on one is attack on all': Pakistan warns Houthis, invokes Mecca defence pact
Article Text:
Pakistan warns Houthis that its defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey

Poll Vote & Share your view What is your opinion on the recent Houthi missile attacks on Saudi Arabia? Justified retaliation Unprovoked aggression Escalation of conflict 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Pakistan warned Tuesday that its newly formed defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could be activated if the conflict in Yemen spills into Saudi territory, saying there should be “no ambiguity” that an attack on any one of the three members would be treated as an attack on all.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif said the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah last month was defensive in nature and required the three countries to respond if any member came under unprovoked aggression.“There should be no ambiguity; there is no need for any clarity that this is a joint defence agreement,” Asif said in an interview with Geo TV. He added that Pakistan was “bound by the terms and conditions of this pact” and would honour its commitments to Saudi Arabia if required.His comments came hours after Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, targeting cities as well as economic and energy infrastructure. At least 73 civilians were injured, according to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen.Asif stressed that the alliance did not give its members a mandate to launch offensive operations against another country on their own initiative.“This is not an aggressive agreement under which the three countries would, on their own initiative, attack another country. But if there is any aggression against one member state, all three member states will respond,” he said.The minister said he was not aware of any contact between Islamabad and Riyadh following the latest Houthi attacks. He also expressed hope that tensions would ease, while warning the Houthis against extending the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia.“If they try to export them, the clauses of this agreement to counter aggression will become operative,” Asif said.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif separately condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as “cowardly” and saying they threatened civilian lives as well as regional peace and security. He said Pakistan stood in “unwavering” solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed support for the kingdom's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity.The Saudi-led coalition said the attacks had temporarily disrupted operations at some targeted sites, while specialised teams worked to contain fires and secure the facilities. Riyadh also warned against continued attacks on civilians and commercial shipping.The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for recent Saudi airstrikes on areas of northwestern Yemen under their control. The group had also accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in Al Hazm on Monday, killing at least 11 people.Asif described the Houthis as “non-state actors” and said sympathy for Iran's position in its ongoing conflict with the United States existed across parts of the Muslim world, including Yemen. But he cautioned against allowing those sentiments to widen the conflict.He also said the Mecca alliance could act as a deterrent without necessarily requiring a military response to every attack.“We don't need to respond to a brick with a stone,” Asif said, arguing that the combined military capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye should themselves serve as a deterrent.
Article Summary: Pakistan warns Houthis that its defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey could be activated if the conflict in Yemen spills into Saudi territory. Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif said the agreement was defensive in nature and required the three countries to respond if any member came under unprovoked aggression.

Article Title: 'Break pattern of impunity': UN experts flag persecution of Pakistan's Ahmadiyya community
Article Text:
Poll Vote & Share your view How should the Pakistani government address human rights violations against minorities? Strengthen laws and policies Increase community awareness programs Collaborate with international organizations All of the above 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

United Nations experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan and urged authorities to ensure their protection.According to an official release, the experts said, "We are deeply concerned by persistent reports that members of the Ahmadiyya community continue to face harassment, criminal prosecution, violence, and exclusion because of their religious identity.""Every individual has the right to freedom of thought, conscience, religion or belief. No one should be subjected to discrimination, intimidation, or violence, nor should they be prevented from peacefully manifesting their faith or face discrimination with respect to any of their human rights," they added.Experts also highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship; desecration of graves; interference with peaceful religious observance, including in the context of Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha; arrests and prosecutions related to religious practices or identity; and hate speech."The State has a responsibility to exercise due diligence to prevent human rights violations, investigate allegations promptly and impartially, prosecute those responsible in accordance with international standards, and provide effective remedies to victims," the experts said.“Pakistan must break the pattern of impunity that has allowed perpetrators of attacks and incitement to hatred and violence to act without restraint,” they said. “These attacks take place with tacit official complicity, whilst the cycle of fear prevents people and institutions from upholding the rights and dignity of these minority groups.”They called on the Pakistan government to ensure that all individuals, regardless of their religion or belief, enjoy equal protection under the law without discrimination. The experts also urged the government to review legislation and administrative measures that may be inconsistent with its obligations under international human rights law, including the rights to freedom of religion or belief, freedom of expression, freedom of association and assembly, cultural rights, and equality before the law."Combating religious intolerance requires more than responding to individual incidents," the release cited them as saying. "It requires sustained efforts to foster respect for diversity, counter incitement to hatred and violence, and create an environment in which all religious or belief communities can live in safety and dignity."
Article Summary: U.N. experts have expressed concerns over reports of human rights violations against members of the Ahmadiyya Muslim community in Pakistan. The experts urged authorities to ensure their protection. They highlighted ongoing attacks on Ahmadi places of worship and desecration of graves.

Article Title: Balochistan’s Zehri under curfew: Civilian killings, detentions and disappearances; what we know
Article Text:
Pakistan's enforced disappearance crisis deepens as four reported missing in Balochistan. Photo credit: ANI

Earlier allegations and UN concerns

A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties.According to a report by The Balochistan Post, Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. Quoting sources,news agency ANI reported that a woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water, while another woman and a man were wounded.Mobile phone services have reportedly been suspended across Zehri, while residents face restrictions on movement. The Balochistan Post said the area has remained under curfew for months, with residents allowed to leave only during designated hours to purchase essential goods. Travel outside the area reportedly requires authorisation from security forces.The Post also reported that Pakistani forces had allegedly killed more than 20 civilians during an operation in the Sohanda area while the curfew was in force.The latest allegations follow a series of reported enforced disappearances elsewhere in Balochistan.On September 2, the local media reported that four people had allegedly gone missing after being detained in Quetta and Dera Bugti, while four previously reported missing persons were recovered from Karachi, Quetta and Hyderabad.The issue has also drawn concern from UN human rights experts. On Saturday, the Office of the UN high commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) raised concerns over the alleged enforced disappearance, torture and extrajudicial killing of Imran Ali.The UN experts said Ali was abducted from his apartment on August 27, 2025, by around 20 personnel from Pakistan’s Counter-Terrorism Department (CTD). They said people previously detained with him later confirmed that he had been held and allegedly tortured.A police officer reportedly told Pakistan’s Commission of Inquiry on Enforced Disappearances in August 2026 that Ali had been killed during an alleged encounter in May. The UN experts called for an independent investigation, forensic examination and identification of six other bodies reportedly brought to a hospital alongside his remains.Meanwhile, Pakistan’s military said on Friday that its forces had killed 48 militants in raids across Mastung, Sibi, Quetta and Kalat over 72 hours, describing those killed as “Khawarij” and “terrorists” without providing evidence, AP reported.
Article Summary: A prolonged curfew and reported military operation in Zehri tehsil of Pakistan’s Balochistan province have triggered fresh allegations of detentions, enforced disappearances and civilian casualties. Pakistani security forces detained around 25 residents from the Sunni area during the operation and allegedly subjected them to enforced disappearance. A woman was also killed in a quadcopter attack while she was collecting water.

Article Title: ‘Growing differences between military, Asif Zardari’: Self-exiled Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain makes big claim
Article Text:
Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain (File photo)

Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari , warning that a debate over creating new provinces could push the country into a major political and security crisis.The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment, which could include provisions for the creation of new provinces.“Discussions on the creation of new provinces have been raised by interior minister Mohsin Naqvi and DG-ISPR. The proposed constitutional changes reflect growing differences between President Asif Ali Zardari and the military leadership. A political deadlock could lead to serious constitutional consequences, including the imposition of martial law or the formation of an interim government,” Hussain said in a TikTok message on September 2.Referring to the earlier 26th and 27th Amendments, he alleged that political parties had previously reached agreements to facilitate their passage.Hussain also questioned the prolonged foreign stay of Zardari, the husband of slain former Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto and father of ex-foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto Zardari."The President had travelled to Austria in connection for his son Bilawal Zardari’s wedding and is currently in London. There was also an hour-long meeting between Zardari and Naqvi in London, claiming that an important message was conveyed to the President," he added.Hussain further cautioned that tensions between the Pakistan military and Sindhi nationalist groups could escalate into widespread unrest. Referring to the situation in Balochistan, Hussain said violence between security forces and Baloch fighters was continuing and called for greater political consideration for the Baloch people.He warned that if Pakistan descended into a broader civil conflict, foreign powers, including the US and UK, would not come to its rescue, and urged Pakistanis to heed his warnings.
Article Summary: Self-exiled British-Pakistani politician Altaf Hussain has alleged a "silent struggle" is underway between Pakistan's powerful military establishment and President Asif Ali Zardari. The founder of the Muttahida Qaumi Movement (MQM) claimed that discussions were underway on a possible 28th Constitutional Amendment.

Article Title: 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in Balochistan attacks, BLA claims
Article Text:
Balochistan: BLA claims 25 Pakistani military personnel killed in two attacks (Picture from X)

The Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) on Thursday claimed responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan’s Balochistan province, saying 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed.According to The Balochistan Post, the BLA spokesperson said fighters targeted a military convoy at Ziarat Cross, attacking vehicles and destroying two of them, including a military truck.The militant group initially claimed that 18 personnel were killed in the attack, with the death toll later rising to 25.The BLA also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal, its official media channel, which it said showed footage from the Ziarat Cross attack.The footage purportedly shows armed fighters near burning Pakistani military vehicles, with bodies visible at the site and weapons being seized. The BLA said it would release the complete video later.In a separate operation in the Hajika area of Surab, the group’s Special Tactical Operations Squad (STOS) remotely detonated an explosives-laden vehicle, destroying a military vehicle and killing seven personnel, according to the BLA statement.
Article Summary: Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA) claims responsibility for two attacks in Pakistan's Balochistan province. BLA says 25 Pakistani military personnel were killed and three military vehicles destroyed. The militant group also released a one-minute-and-11-second video trailer through Hakkal.

Article Title: ‘6ft by 8ft cell, brown drinking water’: What Imran Khan’s jail cell is like
Article Text:

Former Pakistan prime minister Imran Khan is being held in what has been described as harsh conditions at Rawalpindi’s Adiala Jail, with reports alleging prolonged isolation, limited access to reading material and restrictions on contact with his family.According to a report by The Times UK, Khan is being kept in a 6ft by 8ft cell typically used for prisoners on death row. The report said the 73-year-old has no reading material apart from the Quran and is being provided “soiled brown water” to drink.His sons, Sulaiman and Kasim Khan, have reportedly been unable to meet their father in person since 2022 and have at times been prevented from speaking to him by telephone for months. They have described his living conditions as inhumane “torture tactics”.The report said visitors have been barred and Khan has been confined to his cell for as much as 23 hours a day.The reported restrictions have also become the subject of repeated legal challenges by Khan’s family.His sister Uzma Khan filed a fresh contempt petition in the Supreme Court on Wednesday, alleging that authorities have failed to comply with an August 18 order concerning Khan’s access to his family.According to The Express Tribune, the petition names Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, Adiala Jail Superintendent Sajid Baig, Punjab Inspector General of Prisons Mian Salik Jalal and other senior officials as respondents.The August 18 order had directed authorities to facilitate virtual communication between Khan and his sons and allow his sisters to meet him weekly. However, Uzma said she was denied a scheduled visit on Tuesday, while telephone communication between Khan and his sons has remained restricted since March.The petition also alleges that authorities failed to establish the infrastructure required for bi-weekly telephone calls with Sulaiman and Kasim.The latest dispute follows an earlier contempt petition over the alleged non-compliance with the Supreme Court’s direction to transfer Khan to Shifa International Hospital for medical evaluation. He was instead taken to the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) on August 21 before being returned to Adiala Jail after doctors declared him “medically fit”. Authorities have cited security concerns for the decision.
